When the identity of the detainee cannot be ascertained with reasonable certainty.
When the person is so intoxicated he is a danger to himself or others and there is no competent party or agency to assume responsibility for the individual.

When there appears to be a reasonable certainty the detainee will continue or resume the criminal conduct that led to his arrest, or his confinement is necessary for the protection of persons, property or evidence. This exception must be thoroughly documented.
When the arrest is mandated by law, such as for domestic violence.

When the arrest, either on-view or by warrant, is for any of the following offenses of violence: assault, domestic violence, menacing, aggravated menacing, menacing by stalking, aggravated trespass, violation of any Temporary Protection Order, riot, inducing panic, carrying a concealed weapon.
When the detainee has one or more attachments (bench warrants) issued by the Toledo Municipal Court, and there is space available in the Lucas County Pre-Trial Detention Facility.
Police department personnel shall make every reasonable effort to ascertain the true identity of a person who does not have a photo ID, or whose identity is in question.

NOTE: There are many sources to help verify a person’s identity: booking photos, vehicle registration, physical descriptors, search via Accurint, paycheck stub, social security number, personal checks, etc., which when considered in its totality, will help establish a person’s identity.
MISDEMEANOR BOOKING AUTHORIZED
Persons shall be booked for misdemeanors only when:
Arrested for a charge of domestic violence, including on-view arrests and warrants, as well as TPO violations.
Being held for another agency or jurisdiction. (For example, a non-summonsable bench warrant issued by Sylvania or Maumee Court).
Continuation of threatening, violent, or criminal behavior once he has been removed from the scene.
So intoxicated he cannot care for himself and there is no one to care for him.
Identity cannot be reasonably ascertained.
There is an investigative need and a sworn supervisor authorizes booking.
Charged with any offense of violence.
Having one or more attachments and there is space available in the Lucas County Pre-Trial Detention Facility.

NOTE: When a subject is booked, the arrest/booking process should serve all existing warrants as well. Officers shall not issue a summons on selected Toledo Municipal Court charges and book the person on the remaining Toledo Municipal Court charges. This is necessary to prevent duplicate court dates and to reduce scheduling conflicts in the Toledo Municipal Court, Clerk of Courts Office.
TRAFFIC VIOLATIONS
Officers booking persons who also have traffic violations shall write/type “BOOKED” in place of the court date on all E-Citations and paper citations.
ISSUING COURT DATES – ON-VIEW CHARGES
Officers shall not issue court dates when a person is booked for on-view charges and cited for others arising from the same incident.
LCCC booking personnel will issue the court date at the time of release.
REQUEST FOR DENIAL OF OWN RECOGNIZANCE (OR) BOND

During the performance of an officer’s duties, he may become aware of certain information that would justify the denial of an ‘own recognizance’ (OR) bond for specific individuals that have been taken into custody. Such information shall be made available to the LCCC intake officer at the time the subject is booked.
Four primary indicators that may lead officers to request a denial of OR bond are:

blocks.label: (a)
blocks.text: The detainee took extreme measures to avoid apprehension; extended pursuits which endangered the community; or violent resistance to arrest.

blocks.label: (b)
blocks.text: The detainee took extreme measures to avoid detection, as in hiding on a roof or in a small crawl space area.

blocks.label: (c)
blocks.text: The detainee stated or indicated that he would flee if released.

blocks.label: (d)
blocks.text: The detainee indicated, or other information indicates, that he is in such a mental state that he presents a threat or danger to the safety of another person or to the community as a whole.
COMPLETING OWN RECOGNIZANCE (OR) DENIAL REQUEST FORM

When an officer believes that a detainee should not be released on OR Bond, the officer shall complete the REQUEST FOR DENIAL OF OR BOND (TPD FORM 29.6). The form shall be completed in duplicate with the original given to the Intake Officer at LCCC. The duplicate copy shall be attached to the CRIME REPORT or SUPPLEMENTAL CRIME REPORT, depending upon the circumstances (e.g., transporting officers may use a supplemental if they become aware of unique information).
Officers shall clearly state on the form the reason(s) for requesting a denial of OR privileges.
In cases of felony arrests, Investigative Services Division personnel shall forward a copy of this form to the Court Liaison Unit.

blocks.label: (a)
blocks.text: Completion of this form does not insure that a subject will not be released on OR through the Federal Court Order to reduce jail population.
PHOTOGRAPHING AND FINGERPRINTING ADULT ARRESTEES
All adults arrested and booked at the Lucas County Corrections Center shall be photographed and fingerprinted according to Lucas County Corrections Center policy and applicable state law.
ALTERNATIVES TO PHYSICAL ARREST, BOOKING AND/OR CONFINEMENT

The power to arrest that is granted to police officers is one alternative available to officers under circumstances requiring some form of police action. Additional remedies available to officers as alternatives to arrest are issuing a summons in lieu of arrest; summons after arrest without warrant; minor misdemeanor citation; and traffic citation.

Once a violator has been identified, it is the function of the department to initiate the criminal process. However, there are circumstances when a crime may occur and the department will not make a physical arrest. There may be a report written, a sworn complaint made or in some cases when the offense is of a minor nature, a verbal warning, or some other direction given. The decision to not arrest will be governed by department policy and the factual situation involved, not by the personal feelings of the officer. An arrest does not dictate a booking, and a booking does not dictate continued detention.
SUMMONS ARREST
When a summons is issued to a detainee, officers shall follow the procedure outlined above Directive 402.1/3.2 – OPEN MISDEMEANOR WARRANT ARRESTS.
ALL-PURPOSE CITATION (APC)

When an APC is issued to a detainee, officers shall ensure that the APC form is completed and signed by both the detainee and himself. The issuing officer shall also explain to the person that failure to appear in court on the date and time indicated may result in a warrant for his arrest.
Officers, without unnecessary delay, shall swear to and file the original portion of the APC with the clerk of court.
Officers shall turn in the Records Section copy at the end of their shift.
CRIME REPORT REQUIRED FOR SUMMONS AND APC ARREST
Issuing officers shall complete a CRIME REPORT whenever a criminal summons (RECOGNIZANCE – SUMMONS) or APC is issued.
The name of the person receiving the summons shall be placed in the “Suspect Name” field. The court date issued on the summons or APC shall be placed in the F.C.O/Summons Court Date field.

The CRIME REPORT shall also contain a narrative describing the events of the incident. If more than one warrant/attachment is involved, the Record Section numbers and/or case numbers and corresponding offenses shall be listed in the narrative.
LOCAL COURT RULE #17 (MINOR MISDEMEANORS)
Local Court Rule #17 states officers may issue a summons to any person who has a bench warrant (attachment) issued for him if the warrant is for a minor misdemeanor.
Therefore, officers shall not book a person solely on the fact that the person has an attachment for a minor misdemeanor.
CRIMINAL RULE 4 (A) (2) (MISDEMEANOR 1-4)
Most persons arrested on misdemeanor open warrants are eligible to be summoned unless the issuing authority includes a prohibition against it.
INFORMAL RESOLUTION
GENERAL
DISCRETION – In lieu of formal action, when appropriate, an officer may exercise discretion and choose informal action to solve the problem, such as a referral, informal resolution, and warning.

blocks.label: (a)
blocks.text: REFERRALS – An officer may offer the offender a referral to another agency or organization when it is the most reasonable alternative.

blocks.label: (b)
blocks.text: INFORMAL RESOLUTION – An officer may offer informal resolutions to situations and conflicts when they can be adequately resolved through the use of a verbal warnings, referrals, and notification of a parent or guardian of juveniles, etc.

blocks.label: (c)
blocks.text: WARNING – An officer may issue a warning when it is the most reasonable alternative for the offender and the violation.
SOCIAL SERVICE DIVERSION PROGRAMS – ADULTS
MENTAL HEALTH CRISIS SERVICES
Officers may refer persons on a 24-hour basis to the Zepf Center located at 2005 Ashland Avenue in cases involving but not limited to:
Alcohol and drug abuse.
Persons with suicidal tendencies.
Disoriented, hallucinating persons.
Endangered elderly.
Other persons needing guidance or direction in resolving a crisis.
Removed.

summary: The theme of this directive is that **arrest is one option, not the default.** Ohio law and department policy push you toward summons, citation, or informal resolution for misdemeanors, and the directive says it plainly: an arrest does not dictate a booking, and a booking does not dictate continued detention. Misdemeanor booking is only authorized for a specific list of reasons (section 3.5).

Felony arrestees go to the Investigations Bureau first, not straight to the jail. The ISB supervisor handles interrogation, case review, prosecutor contact, DNA collection, and the Felony Booking Authorization Form, without which LCCC will not accept the prisoner.
The directive also covers Miranda, foreign nationals (consular notification), consular immunity, arrests of city employees, mistaken arrests, and requests to deny OR bond.
must: Tell a warrantless arrestee your authority and the cause of arrest, unless they were caught in the act (Policy)
Give Miranda before any custodial questioning, misdemeanor or felony (1.1)

For a foreign national you arrest or detain: get name, DOB and country, notify the on-duty Records supervisor, note that supervisor's name in your report, and tell the person they may contact their embassy. Some countries require embassy notification even if the person declines; Records keeps that list (1.4)

Call a sworn supervisor to the scene before releasing anyone you have arrested without charges. The supervisor explains the release and arranges a ride; you write a Crime Report and the supervisor writes an Unusual Incident Report (1.5.1)
Notify the watch commander immediately if a mistaken arrest is discovered after booking (1.5.2)
Take felony arrestees to the Investigations Section before the jail, for interrogation, DNA sample if their CCH is not flagged, and the Felony Booking Authorization Form (TPD 61.2) (2.1, 2.2)

Review every on-view misdemeanor arrest for release by summons or citation, run a records check for prior convictions that elevate the charge or for other wants, and re-check your booking decision at the jail before booking (3.1.1 to 3.1.3)
Have the officer who witnessed the violation sign all affidavits, summonses, APCs and citations for that detainee (3.1.5)

Use the Recognizance-Summons for summonsable misdemeanor warrants: court date 7 to 10 days out, tell Records the date and time, one form per court, check the Multiple Cases box when it applies (3.2.4)
Write a Crime Report every time you issue a criminal summons or APC, with the court date in the F.C.O/Summons field (4.3)
Swear to and file the original APC with the clerk without unnecessary delay, and turn in the Records copy at end of shift (4.2)
Write a Sergeant's Report (TPD 20.7) when you arrest a City of Toledo employee and send it to the Personnel Section commander (1.3)
Give the LCCC intake officer any information justifying denial of OR bond, on a Request for Denial of OR Bond form (TPD 29.6), original to intake and a copy on your report (3.8, 3.9)
never: Release an arrestee without charges on your own; a sworn supervisor must authorize it (1.5.1a)
Book someone solely on a minor misdemeanor attachment (4.4.1)
Summons a person on some Toledo Municipal Court charges and book them on others from the same court; if any TMC warrant is non-summonsable, book on all TMC warrants (3.2.4j, 3.5 note)
Summons a defendant into multiple courts on the same date and time (3.2.4h)
Issue court dates on citations when the person is being booked on other charges from the same incident; write BOOKED in place of the court date, and LCCC sets the date at release (3.6, 3.7)
File a felony affidavit for a non-custody suspect without the Investigations Bureau supervisor and county prosecutor's authorization (2.4)
Arrest a consular officer for a criminal or traffic offense unless a federal magistrate orders it (1.2)
notes: Misdemeanor booking is authorized only when: domestic violence or TPO violation; held for another agency; continued threatening or criminal behavior after removal from the scene; too intoxicated to care for self with no one to take them; identity cannot reasonably be determined; investigative need with a sworn supervisor's approval; any offense of violence; or a TMC attachment with Pre-Trial Detention bed space available (3.5)
Offenses of violence for the booking exception include assault, DV, menacing, aggravated menacing, menacing by stalking, aggravated trespass, TPO violation, riot, inducing panic, and CCW (3.4.1)
Attachments (bench warrants) from Toledo Municipal Court mean booking at Pre-Trial Detention if a bed is available; Records calls LCCC first, and if no bed, you summons (3.3)

DNA collection is required for all adult felony arrestees unless their CCH shows a DNA flag. If the arrestee refuses, notify an investigative supervisor, who decides between forced collection and booking under the standing court order that holds them until they provide a sample (2.3)
Indicators for an OR denial request: extreme measures to avoid apprehension, hiding to avoid detection, stated intent to flee, or a mental state that makes them a danger (3.8.2)

Informal resolution (referral, warning, parent notification) is an accepted outcome when it reasonably solves the problem; the Zepf Center at 2005 Ashland takes 24-hour mental health, substance abuse and crisis referrals (5)
You do not have to drive a released detainee back to where you picked them up, but you may if it is the decent thing to do (3.1.3 note)

directives.title: Search and Seizure Without a Warrant

blocks.text: Policy

The Toledo Police Department is responsive to the needs and constitutional rights of the community and develops public confidence by carrying out the police function in an ethical and lawful manner. The department operates under written rules imposed by the U.S. Supreme Court as well as federal, state and local court decisions governing search and seizure. The following procedures are meant to be guidelines for use by officers of this department.
Procedures
SEARCH BY CONSENT

Officers do not need a search warrant when an individual voluntarily consents to a search. Consent is not an exception to the warrant requirement, but a decision by a citizen not to assert Fourth Amendment rights.
The consent must be voluntarily given.
In the search of a residence or apartment, a spouse or co-tenant with a right to access may consent to the search of the common areas only.
A landlord or hotel employee cannot give consent to the search of a rented apartment or room.
Silence does not imply consent.
Coercion may not be used.
Whenever possible, a written waiver of search should be obtained.
STOP AND FRISK

When an officer observes a situation where the actions of a person lead him/her to believe that criminal activity may be occurring or may have occurred, the officer has the right and duty to make an investigatory stop.
If while the stop is being conducted officers feel that they have articulable reasons to fear for their safety, i.e. the person may be armed; the person may be patted down for weapons.
Facts observed by an officer may be combined with the following to justify a stop:
Surrounding circumstances, such as time and location of stop;
Rational inferences drawn from facts, circumstances;
Officer's past experience and prior knowledge; and/or

Information from other sources, including reliable informants. NOTE: Officers shall not stop, detain, question or arrest a person based solely on characteristics of race, ethnicity or gender, gender identity, or sexual orientation.
AUTOMOBILE SEARCHES
May be conducted without a warrant when:
Probable cause exists to believe evidence of a crime will be found.
Facts giving rise to probable cause must be such that they would support issuance of a search warrant.

Where a married person has sufficient rights of common access, use, and control of a vehicle registered in his/her spouse's name, he/she has authority to consent to the search of the vehicle against the wishes of the other.
Automobile inventories will be conducted according to Directive 406.3 – TOWS.
CRIME SCENE SEARCH

During the initial response to a crime scene, officers may make a warrantless entry to render immediate aid to victims and may also conduct a warrantless search for suspects, any further search must be conducted by warrant or fall within one of the established exceptions to the warrant requirement, as specified in the Ohio Revised Code or the Ohio Rules of Criminal Procedure.
EXIGENT CIRCUMSTANCES

Those circumstances that would cause a reasonable person to believe that entry, or other prompt action was necessary to prevent physical harm to officers or other persons, the destruction of evidence, the escape of a suspect, or some other consequence improperly frustrating legitimate law enforcement efforts.

Entry of a residence to conduct a search, even for a person, must be conducted with a warrant, absent exigent circumstances. Factors to be considered as to whether there is an emergency that will permit a warrantless intrusion into a home to investigate, are:
Probable cause exists to believe the offense is a crime of violence;
It is reasonably believed that the suspect is armed;
There is strong reason to believe that the suspect is on the premises;
It is likely that the suspect will escape if not swiftly apprehended.

If an officer is in hot pursuit of a person and observed him enter a secured area, the officer may pursue the person into that area to effect a warrantless arrest. The term "hot pursuit", shall be defined as, immediate and continuous pursuit from the moment probable cause arose to arrest.
SEARCH – INCIDENT TO ARREST
Officers may search incident to arrest without a warrant, provided the arrest is valid and the arrestee is taken into custody.
The area and possessions within the arrestee's immediate control may be searched for weapons and/or evidence.
SEARCH – PLAIN VIEW
Warrantless seizures involving evidence of crime in plain view are not prohibited by the fourth amendment where the incriminatory nature of an object is immediately apparent.
Discovery of such evidence should be inadvertent.
ABANDONED PROPERTY
Officers may search and seize property that they reasonably believe has been abandoned.

summary: A short directive that lists the warrant exceptions the department recognizes: consent, stop and frisk, automobile searches on probable cause, crime-scene emergency entry, exigent circumstances and hot pursuit, search incident to arrest, plain view, and abandoned property. It is written as guidelines, and it points to the Ohio Revised Code and Criminal Rules for anything it does not cover. The core message is simple: a home gets a warrant unless a real emergency exists, and consent only counts when it is truly voluntary.

Last revised in 2016, so the directive does not reflect later case law on topics like cell phones (Riley) or vehicle searches of digital devices. Where the directive is silent, current Fourth Amendment law controls.
must: Get a warrant to enter a residence to search, even for a person, unless exigent circumstances exist (5.1)
Make sure consent is voluntary; try to get a written waiver whenever possible (1.2, 1.5)
Limit a co-tenant's or spouse's consent to the common areas they have a right to access (1.2.1)
Have articulable reasons to fear for your safety before patting someone down during an investigatory stop (2.2)
Have probable cause that would support a warrant before searching a vehicle without one; inventories follow 406.3 Tows (3)
Limit a search incident to arrest to the arrestee's immediate control area and possessions, and only when the arrest is valid and the person is actually taken into custody (6, 6.1)
After the initial emergency entry and sweep at a crime scene, stop and get a warrant or fit a recognized exception before searching further (4)
never: Treat silence as consent (1.3)
Use coercion to get consent (1.4)
Accept consent from a landlord or hotel employee for a rented apartment or room (1.2.2)
Stop, detain, question or arrest anyone based solely on race, ethnicity, gender, gender identity or sexual orientation (2.3.4 note)
notes: Reasonable suspicion for a stop can be built from what you see plus time and location, rational inferences, your experience and knowledge, and information from reliable sources (2.3)

Exigency factors for a warrantless home entry: probable cause for a crime of violence, reason to believe the suspect is armed, strong reason to believe the suspect is inside, and likely escape if you wait (5.1.1 to 5.1.4)
Hot pursuit means immediate and continuous pursuit from the moment probable cause to arrest arose. If you watch the suspect go into a secured area, you can follow (5.2)
Plain view requires the incriminating nature to be immediately apparent, and the discovery should be inadvertent (7)
A spouse with common access, use and control of a vehicle can consent to its search even over the other spouse's objection (3)

blocks.text: Policy
The United States Supreme Court has addressed one-on-one identification in numerous cases and has set forth guidelines to be followed when officers solicit eyewitness identification.
Procedures
GENERAL GUIDELINES

A primary consideration is the time period between the time the offense was reported and the discovery of the suspect. No one-on-one identification shall be attempted if the suspect is not stopped initially within an hour of the offense. (The clock stops when the suspect is stopped; however, the detention clock starts at this time. See 2.2 below.)

The distance between the crime scene and the point the suspect is located shall not be excessive considering the totality of the circumstances – i.e., the time of day, the mode of transportation, etc.
The identification process shall be conducted so as not to be unnecessarily suggestive or conducive to irreparable mistaken identity.
Officers shall take into consideration:

The similarities of age, race, clothing, height, weight, speech characteristics and any other personal identifier shall be reasonably correlated between the suspect stopped and description of the suspect, considering the collective information available.
The totality of knowledge of the critical events known to the police at the point the suspect is stopped.
The degree of opportunity and attention the victim/witness had in reference to the suspects.
ONE-ON-ONE IDENTIFICATION PROCESS

The detective assigned to the case shall be notified and, if available shall conduct the one-on-one identification process. If no investigator is available, a uniformed command officer shall conduct the process. The investigator shall have the ultimate authority to direct the identification process, regardless of rank.
The detention of the suspect should not exceed twenty minutes.

Witnesses shall view the suspect one at a time. No viewer, police officer, or bystander shall be permitted to voice an opinion relative to the suspect being viewed and his/her relationship to the victim or offense involved.

The witness shall be transported to the suspect's location. In an emergency situation, such as the victim being in danger of dying, an immediate identification confrontation may be conducted, with the permission of medical authorities, by conveying the suspect to the crime scene or medical facility.
When following this practice, it is important that the conveying officers avoid implicating anyone either through verbal suggestion or physical gesture.

Documentation of an identification procedure and the manner in which it was conducted may be important in suppression hearings, trials and post-conviction appeals. Therefore, the assigned investigator or command officer conducting the identification process shall complete a SUPPLEMENTAL REPORT (TPD FORM 38.3). The SUPPLEMENTAL shall include the following:
The time, date and location of the identification procedure.
A record of everyone present, including those not viewing the suspect.
A description of where the suspect was positioned relative to police vehicles and officers, and any utterances made.
All statements made by the viewer, the command officer or investigator, and any other person present.
A notation of the time period between the initial stopping of the suspect and the completion of the identification process.
If the suspect was handcuffed, during the one-on-one identification, the reason shall be documented in the supplemental report.

No one-on-one identification confrontation shall be conducted when the suspect is in a department vehicle, or is in a position where the witness can see the suspect being frisked or searched by police officers.

During a one-on-one identification, the suspect should not be handcuffed when a witness can observe the suspect. However, due to the totality of the circumstances, i.e. flight risk or combativeness of the suspect, whether the suspect is handcuffed or not, is left to the discretion of the detective assigned the case or the uniformed command officer in charge of the one-on-one identification.

The one-on-one identification confrontation has not been legally classified as a "critical stage" in the pre-arrest process. Therefore, the suspect does not have the right to an attorney. If the suspect's attorney is present, he shall be permitted to view the identification proceedings and take notes, but he cannot make suggestions or demands relative to the proceedings.

summary: A one-on-one (show-up) identification is inherently suggestive, so the directive puts hard limits on when and how it happens. The suspect must be stopped within an hour of the offense and reasonably close to the scene, the detention is capped at about twenty minutes, the witness is brought to the suspect (not the other way around, except in a medical emergency), and the whole thing is run and documented by the case detective or a uniformed command officer.
must: Stop the suspect within one hour of the offense or do not attempt a show-up at all. The detention clock starts when the suspect is stopped (1.1)
Keep the distance from the scene reasonable given time of day and mode of travel, and make sure the suspect reasonably matches the description (1.2, 1.4.1)
Notify the assigned detective; the detective runs the show-up if available, otherwise a uniformed command officer does. The investigator has final authority regardless of rank (2.1)
Keep the detention to about twenty minutes (2.2)
Have witnesses view the suspect one at a time, in silence; nobody present voices an opinion (2.3)
Transport the witness to the suspect. Only move the suspect to the scene or hospital in an emergency, such as a dying victim, with medical permission (2.4)

Document everything in a Supplemental Report (TPD 38.3): time, date, location, everyone present, where the suspect stood relative to cars and officers, every statement made, elapsed time, and the reason if the suspect was handcuffed (2.5)
never: Show the suspect while they are inside a police vehicle, or where the witness can see them being frisked or searched (2.6)
Handcuff the suspect in view of the witness unless flight risk or combativeness justifies it, and then document why (2.7)
Suggest anything to the witness by word or gesture (2.4.1, 2.3)
notes: The suspect has no right to counsel at a show-up. If their attorney happens to be present, they may watch and take notes but cannot direct the process (2.8)
Consider how good a look the witness actually got; opportunity and attention matter to whether the identification will hold up (1.4.3)

directives.title: Strip Search and Body Cavity Search

blocks.text: Policy
It is the policy of the department to conduct all strip or body cavity searches within the guidelines of the Ohio Revised Code (ORC) 2933.32.
Definitions

The ORC 2933.32, defines strip search as an inspection of the genitalia, buttocks, breasts, or undergarments of a person that is preceded by the removal or rearrangement of some or all of the person’s clothing that directly covers the person’s genitalia, buttocks, breasts or undergarments and that is conducted visually, manually, by means of any instrument, apparatus or object, or in any other manner.
The ORC 2933.32, defines body cavity search as an inspection of the anal or vaginal cavity manually, by means of any instrument, apparatus or object, or in any other manner.
Procedures
SEARCH RESTRICTION

No member of the department who has detained or arrested a person for the alleged commission of a misdemeanor or traffic offense shall conduct or cause to be conducted a strip search of said person, unless there is probable cause to believe that the person is concealing evidence of the commission of a criminal offense, including fruits or tools of a crime, contraband, or a deadly weapon, that would not otherwise be discovered.

A body cavity search shall be conducted only after a search warrant is issued that authorizes the search, and shall only be conducted under sanitary conditions by a physician, registered nurse, or licensed practical nurse.

The appropriate ranking on-duty Investigative Services Division command officer shall be responsible for contacting the Lucas County Corrections Center to arrange for medical personnel at the jail to conduct the body cavity search after the search warrant has been obtained.

In addition to any search warrant that may have been obtained, no member of the department shall conduct a strip or a body cavity search until a written authorization (AUTHORIZATION TO PERFORM BODY CAVITY OR STRIP SEARCH TPD FORM 30.4) is completed by the appropriate ranking on-duty Investigative Services Division command officer.

A strip or body cavity search shall be conducted by a person or persons who are of the same sex as the person who is being searched. The search shall be conducted in a manner and in a location that permits only the person or persons who are physically conducting the search to observe the search.

When a discrepancy exists between a person’s appearance, government-issued identification, and/or any law enforcement database record, officers shall ask the person how the person identifies and attempt to accommodate the person.
REPORTS REQUIRED
Upon completion of any search pursuant to this section, the officer who conducted or caused to be conducted the search shall prepare a CRIME REPORT (TPD FORM 38.1), including all of the following:
The name, sex, date of birth and social security number of the person who was searched.
The time, date, and location of the search.
The names of the officers who conducted the search, their four digit identification number, their sex and current assignment.
A list of any items recovered during the search.
The facts upon which the officers based their probable cause for the search.

Officers shall attach the AUTHORIZATION TO PERFORM BODY CAVITY OR STRIP SEARCH, to the CRIME REPORT. The officers who conducted the search shall then furnish a copy of the CRIME REPORT, the authorization form, and any report of the medical personnel to the person who was searched.

summary: Strip searches and body cavity searches are governed by ORC 2933.32, and this directive tracks the statute. A strip search means any exposure or rearrangement of clothing covering the genitals, buttocks, breasts or undergarments for inspection. A body cavity search is a manual or instrument inspection of the anal or vaginal cavity. The bar is high for both, the paperwork is mandatory, and the person searched gets a copy of everything.
must: Have probable cause that the person is hiding evidence, contraband or a deadly weapon that would not otherwise be found before strip searching anyone detained or arrested for a misdemeanor or traffic offense (1.1)

Get a search warrant before any body cavity search, and have it performed by a physician, RN or LPN under sanitary conditions. The ranking on-duty ISD command officer arranges medical personnel at the Lucas County Corrections Center (1.2, 1.2.1)

Get a completed written Authorization to Perform Body Cavity or Strip Search (TPD 30.4) from the ranking on-duty Investigative Services Division command officer before any strip or body cavity search, even if you already have a warrant (1.3)
Use searchers of the same sex as the person, in a place where only the people conducting the search can see (1.4)
If appearance, ID and database records do not match, ask the person how they identify and try to accommodate them (1.5)

Write a Crime Report (TPD 38.1) with the person's name, sex, DOB and SSN; time, date and location; names, badge numbers, sex and assignment of the searching officers; items recovered; and the facts supporting probable cause (2.1)
Attach the authorization form to the Crime Report, and give the person a copy of the report, the authorization, and any medical report (2.2)
never: Strip search a misdemeanor or traffic arrestee as routine practice (1.1)
Perform a body cavity search yourself, or without a warrant (1.2)
Conduct either search without the TPD 30.4 authorization in hand (1.3)
Let anyone who is not physically conducting the search observe it (1.4)
notes: Remember the definition: making someone pull their waistband out or lift a bra to look is a strip search under the statute, with all the same requirements.

The directive is silent on felony arrestees' strip searches beyond the general rules in sections 1.3 and 1.4, so the authorization form and same-sex, private-location rules apply to every strip search regardless of charge.

blocks.text: Policy

To ensure the safety of all officers and detainees, the following procedures shall be established to detail accountability and the documentation of detainees delivered to, detained, and/or removed from department facilities.
Definitions

A detainee containment compartment installed in some patrol wagons, which is constructed of solid metal and includes a video surveillance system. INTERIOR SHIELD – A vehicle partition installed in patrol sedans, which separates the passenger compartment into two separate areas; the front area for officers and the rear area for subjects, suspects and detainees.
A physician, registered nurse, certified nurse-midwife or a physician assistance.
The period of recovery immediately following childbirth, miscarriage or termination of a pregnancy up to six weeks after the pregnancy.
Use of shackles, handcuffs or other similar appliance or device.
Procedures
DETAINEE SEARCHES
DETAINEE SEARCHES

Prior to transporting a detainee, the arresting officer shall be held strictly accountable for making a proper and thorough search. In every instance, the following property shall be removed from the possession of a detainee:
Property carried unlawfully.
Any weapons or dangerous instruments.
Property lawfully carried but dangerous to life, or which could facilitate escape.
Property required as evidence.
Property taken from a detainee shall be handled in accordance with existing procedures for disposition of property.
TRANSPORTING OFFICER SEARCH

If the transporting officer is not the arresting officer, he should not assume that the detainee has been properly searched. For his own safety, prior to placing the detainee into a vehicle, the transporting officer shall thoroughly search the detainee.
OPPOSITE SEX DETAINEES

If there are reasonable grounds to believe that a detainee of the opposite sex is carrying a concealed weapon or dangerous instrument, the officer, for his own safety, shall search the detainee prior to transport.

Anytime a detainee of the opposite sex is to be searched, a reasonable attempt shall be made to have the search conducted by an officer of the same sex. If an officer of the same sex is not available, the search shall be conducted in the presence of a witness.

In all cases when a detainee is transported, regardless of sex, the odometer reading, location and destination shall be reported by radio to the dispatcher, prior to the transporting officers leaving the scene. Upon arrival at the destination, the odometer reading shall again be given by radio. The location of pickup, the destination, the time the vehicle left the pickup point, the time the vehicle arrived at the destination and both odometer readings shall be recorded by the dispatcher.
At no time shall an officer use the trip odometer as an odometer reading. The officer shall use the actual odometer reading as it appears.
TRANSPORTING DETAINEES
HANDCUFFING

The use of handcuffs is mandatory on all detainees regardless if a unit is a two man or one man unit. The preferred method of handcuffing is with the detainee’s hands behind the back, or one of the accepted variations for multiple arrests.
A detainee shall not be handcuffed in front. Handcuffs shall not be used as a come-along. A detainee shall not be handcuffed to any officer.

EXCEPTION: Should a detainee have a deformity or injury that would prevent handcuffing in the prescribed manner, restraints shall be applied in such a way as to prevent injury or cause additional injury.

Should it be necessary for a detainee to be handcuffed in front, his hands should be further restrained to reduce the chance of the handcuffs being used as a weapon (e.g., secure handcuffs to the detainee’s belt or belt loop on his pants).

A department-issued hobbling device may be used by an officer to secure a combative detainee when the detainee poses a threat to himself or others, or could cause significant damage to property if not properly restrained. The following procedure applies to the use of hobbling devices:

blocks.label: (a)
blocks.text: Detainees transported in a patrol wagon shall be accompanied and guarded in the rear confinement area/internal security compartment by the second officer of the transporting unit or, in OVI cases, by the arresting officer. Detainees shall be placed in a seated position on the floor of the confinement area with the officer seated behind the detainee.

blocks.label: (b)
blocks.text: A sworn supervisor shall be notified before transporting any detainee restrained with a hobbling device.
In no instance shall an officer shackle directly together a detainee’s hands and ankles (hog-tying), nor shall a detainee’s feet be hobbled by a restraint that is secured behind the back.

Whenever an officer removes a detainee from the custody of a detention or medical facility and transports them to another location, the detainee shall remain handcuffed during the transport (e.g., transport to Investigations Bureau, Records Section, Identification Unit).
In instances where detainees are in an interview room and an investigator has reason to believe a greater degree of cooperation may be achieved in the interrogation, the handcuffs may be removed.
HANDCUFFING/INJURY
In all instances where restraining devices are used, they shall be used in such a way as to minimize the chance of injury or unnecessary discomfort upon the detainee being restrained.
POSITIONAL ASPHYXIA

Positional asphyxia occurs when a subject’s body is placed in a position that interferes with breathing. Several factors, including a violent struggle with an officer, particularly when the use of behind the back handcuffing is combined with placing the detainee in a stomach-down prone position, could increase the risk of positional asphyxia. Therefore:
Any detainee placed in a stomach-down prone position while handcuffed shall be closely monitored for breathing difficulties and/or other medical considerations.
Once a detainee is controlled, he shall immediately be placed either in a seated position or placed in a position lying on his side with the legs no closer than a 90-degree angle to the torso.

No detainee shall be transported in a stomach-down prone position while handcuffed, except as a last resort, when its use becomes necessary to prevent the detainee from injuring himself or the transporting officer.
PATROL WAGONS
Patrol wagons shall be the preferred means of transporting detainees. Detainees shall be transported in a wagon when one is readily available.

When transporting a detainee in a patrol wagon that is not equipped with an internal security compartment, the detainee shall be accompanied and guarded in the rear confinement area by the second officer of the transporting unit or, in OVI cases, by the arresting officer.
When transporting a detainee in a patrol wagon equipped with an internal security compartment:

blocks.label: (a)
blocks.text: Officers are not required to ride in the rear compartment with the detainee unless one of the following exceptions applies:
A detainee is being transported in a stomach-down prone position.
A detainee is not seat-belted securely to the bench seat.
A detainee is being restrained with a hobbling device.
A spit hood is being used on a detainee
A sick or injured detainee is being transported to a medical facility, hospital or other location.
A detainee is under arrest for OVI.
The video surveillance system used to monitor detainees is not functioning properly.

blocks.label: (b)
blocks.text: During transport, officers shall monitor the detainee either through the video surveillance system, or accompanying and guarding the detainee in the Internal Security Compartment.

blocks.label: (c)
blocks.text: A detainee shall not be placed in any compartment that contains any police-related equipment or officer’s personal belongings.

blocks.label: (d)
blocks.text: All detainees shall be seat-belted securely to the bench. In those instances where the detainee’s demeanor or physical condition (e.g., sick, intoxicated) precludes riding in a seated position on the bench, seat belting of the detainee is not required. However, the detainee shall be accompanied and guarded in the internal security compartment by the second officer and the reasons for transporting the detainee without seat belting shall be documented in the CRIME REPORT (TPD FORM 38.1).

blocks.label: (e)
blocks.text: The interior security door of the internal security compartment shall be completely closed and locked during transportation.
EXCEPTION: The interior security door shall not be locked during transportation when an officer accompanies a detainee in the Internal Security Compartment.
No officer shall ride on the outside of the vehicle.
PATROL SEDANS

Situations may arise where it is not practical to use a patrol wagon to transport a detainee. In these cases, a patrol sedan may be used to expedite the transportation of the detainee. The determination on whether to transport a detainee in a wagon or sedan shall be made by the arresting officer or a sworn supervisor.
If a detainee is transported in a police sedan the following procedure shall be followed:

blocks.label: (a)
blocks.text: The detainee shall ride on the passenger side of the rear seat and shall be seat-belted securely. At no time shall a detainee ride in the front seat of a patrol sedan.

blocks.label: (b)
blocks.text: If a metal screen is not installed as part of the interior shield, the interior shield shall be closed.

blocks.label: (c)
blocks.text: If part of a two man unit, the non-driving officer has the option to sit in the front seat or the left side of the rear seat behind the driver. However, at all times the non-driving officer maintains the primary responsibility and accountability for the safety and security of the detainee and the officers.

One man units are discouraged from transporting multiple detainees. However, it remains the responsibility of the transporting officer to determine if he can safely transport multiple detainees. If the one man unit believes there is a danger in transporting more than one detainee, he shall notify the dispatcher and request assistance in transporting.
SEDANS WITHOUT INTERIOR SHIELDS
Anytime an officer transports a detainee in a sedan (either marked or unmarked), that does not have an interior shield, the following procedure shall be followed:
The detainee shall ride on the passenger side of the rear seat and shall be seat-belted securely. At no time shall a detainee ride in the front seat of a sedan.

If part of a two man unit, the non-driving officer has the option to sit in the front seat or the left side of the rear seat behind the driver. However, at all times the non-driving officer maintains the primary responsibility and accountability for the safety and security of the detainee and the officers.
If the one man unit believes there is a danger in transporting the detainee, he shall notify the dispatcher and request assistance in transporting.
VEHICLE SEARCH

Prior to placing a detainee in a department vehicle, the vehicle shall be searched for weapons and contraband. After the detainee has reached the appropriate destination and is secure, the officers shall again search the vehicle for any weapons or contraband that may have been left behind by the detainee.
MONITORING OF DETAINEE AND THE USE OF SPIT HOODS

A detainee shall not be placed in a patrol wagon or police sedan and left unattended unless a life-threatening situation or other emergency arises that the officer must respond to or take action upon. Transporting officers remain responsible for the safety of detainees. A department-issued spit hood may be used to prevent the transfer of spit from a detainee to others. The following procedure applies to the use of spit hoods:
Spit hoods shall only be used when a detainee is spitting or threatening to spit
Spit hoods shall not be used on any detainee who is in respiratory distress, vomiting, requires medical attention or is unconscious.
Officers shall constantly monitor any detainee wearing a spit hood.
The use of a spit hood shall be documented in the CRIME REPORT and any other required reports.
DETAINEE COMMUNICATION WITH OTHERS

To help reduce the chance of injury or escape by a detainee during transportation, an officer shall not stop to allow a detainee to communicate with family, friends or his attorney. Once the detainee is in a secure location (e.g., Lucas County Correction Center, Investigations Bureau) he may be afforded the opportunity to speak to those individuals.
DETAINEE ESCAPE

Should a detainee escape while in the custody of an officer, the officer shall immediately notify the dispatcher of the situation. Notification shall include the location and direction of flight, description of the detainee, charges and other information related to officer safety and to aid in the apprehension of the detainee. The following procedure shall be followed:
The officer shall then notify his immediate supervisor.

The officer shall complete the required CRIME REPORT and articulate the facts and circumstances of the escape. A supervisor may also require the officer to complete a SUPPLEMENTAL CRIME REPORT (TPD FORM 38.3).
Should a detainee escape from an officer's custody while outside of the city of Toledo, a Communications supervisor shall notify the agency that has jurisdiction where the escape occurred.
The officer shall follow the orders of the supervisor regarding any further actions that may be required.
SICK OR INJURED DETAINEES
When it becomes apparent that a detainee is sick/injured and needs medical attention, the following procedure shall be followed:

Depending on the urgency of the detainee’s need for medical attention, officers shall either request assistance from the Toledo Fire and Rescue Department or transport the detainee immediately to the nearest hospital with EMS approval.
If the detainee is transported to a hospital in a non-department vehicle (e.g., Life Squad, ambulance), at least one officer shall remain with the detainee at all times.

An officer shall remain with the detainee at all times while at the hospital. If a medical procedure being performed is potentially dangerous to the officer, or if the physician requests that the officer leave, he may wait outside the treatment area. However, the officer shall ensure the detainee does not escape.

If a physician requests the officer remove the handcuffs from a detainee to facilitate medical treatment, the officer may remove the handcuffs. However, the officer shall ensure the detainee does not escape.
Individuals arrested only on misdemeanor charges and detained for a prolonged treatment period, or admitted to the hospital, shall be issued a summons in accordance with established procedures.
An officer who transports a detainee from a hospital to the Lucas County Corrections Center (LCCC) shall convey any medical instructions for the proper care of the detainee to LCCC personnel.
HOSPITALIZATION/VISITATION OF DETAINEE

If an individual arrested on felony charges is admitted to the hospital, the officer having custody of the detainee shall immediately notify an Investigations Bureau supervisor. If a supervisor is not on-duty, he shall contact an appropriate on-duty detective who will determine if guard protection is deemed necessary.
When notified of a detainee’s admission and confinement to a hospital, Investigations Bureau personnel shall:

blocks.label: (a)
blocks.text: Assess the degree of risk, isolation needs, type of treatment, and all other pertinent information in order to determine the amount and type of security necessary.

blocks.label: (b)
blocks.text: Determine the approximate length of time the detainee will be hospitalized.

blocks.label: (c)
blocks.text: Coordinate with Operations Division supervisors to provide a rotating work schedule of Operations Division personnel to guard the detainee.

blocks.label: (d)
blocks.text: At shift change, provide relieving Operations Division personnel with all pertinent information necessary for continued guard duty of the hospitalized detainee.

Watch commanders shall assign officers to guard duty during their regular shift, unless advised differently by the Operations Division commander or chief of police. Guard duty shifts should be no longer than eight (8) hours.
The officer assigned to guard a hospitalized detainee shall:

blocks.label: (a)
blocks.text: Remain with the detainee continuously and monitor all personal contacts.

blocks.label: (b)
blocks.text: Be alert to prevent suicide, escape, and/or assault attempts. Restraining devices may be used, if deemed necessary.

blocks.label: (c)
blocks.text: Prevent unauthorized property from being passed to the detainee.

blocks.label: (d)
blocks.text: If practical, the detainee shall be searched and restrained prior to being moved or transferred within the hospital.

blocks.label: (e)
blocks.text: Consult an Investigations Bureau supervisor for instructions when uncertain regarding specific procedures.
VISITATION

All persons wishing to visit a hospitalized detainee must obtain the appropriate pass at the Investigative Bureau desk located at the Safety Building. An Investigations Bureau sworn supervisor, following the guidelines and procedures set forth in the Investigations Bureau Manual, shall insure that the guarded detainee is advised of the visitation policy.
VISITATION PASSES ISSUED

An Investigations Bureau sworn supervisor shall issue all passes. Visitors must apply in person and present a valid state-issued photo identification. A copy of all issued passes shall be maintained as a permanent record in the case file. The following types of passes may be issued:

HOSPITAL VISITATION PASS (TPD FORM 31.4) – This pass is valid for only one visit on the day the pass is issued. Therefore, the guarding officer shall retain the yellow copy of the pass and forward it to the Investigations Bureau at the end of his shift.

CLERGY HOSPITAL VISITATION PASS (TPD FORM 31.45) – This pass is valid for multiple visits with the guarded detainee. Members of the clergy shall be allowed to retain the yellow copy of their pass. However, they are still required to present the pass and valid state-issued photo identification at each visit.
VISITATION LIMITATIONS

When guarding a detainee who is admitted to an area hospital, officers shall not allow a detainee visitation unless presented with the yellow copy of either the HOSPITAL VISITATION PASS or CLERGY HOSPITAL VISITATION PASS and a valid stateissued photo identification. The guarding officer shall verify that the name on the issued pass matches the person wishing to visit the detainee.

Officers assigned to guard duty shall direct all visitors without a pass to the Investigations Bureau desk located at the Safety Building. Visitation of detainees under guard by the Toledo Police Department shall be limited to clergy, attorneys or immediate family members (e.g., mother, father, spouse, brother, sister or adult children).
Visitation shall be limited to one person at a time.
Detainees shall be limited to two visitors per day, including family and attorneys. Visits from members of the clergy are excluded from this limitation.
Each visit shall not exceed 30 minutes.
All visitors are subject to a “pat down” search of their persons and a thorough search of purses, packages, and any item intended to be left for the detainee.
Visitation is limited to those hours established by the hospital or unit where the detainee is currently being treated.

EXCEPTION: Imminent death of the detainee. If medical personnel summon family members to the hospital due to the imminent death of the detainee, the officers guarding the detainee shall immediately notify an Investigations Bureau sworn supervisor for instructions.

Even if the visitor has been issued a pass, the guarding officer can still deny visitation when: ο The visitor’s presence in the hospital constitutes a clear and probable danger to hospital security or interferes with hospital operations. ο The visitor is under the influence of drugs or alcohol. ο The visitor refuses or fails to show proper identification. ο The visitor refuses to submit to a pat down or search of belongings. ο The visitor’s past behavior was disruptive.
DISABLED DETAINEES

Should the need arise to transport a disabled detainee or special needs detainee, a patrol wagon shall be utilized whenever available. If a patrol wagon is not available, the officer shall contact his supervisor for instructions.
For safety considerations, officers are reminded that not all individuals in wheel chairs are immobile. Some people utilizing wheelchairs are capable of walking.
A wheelchair is a piece of medical equipment and shall not be relied upon to serve as a restraining device.
DETAINEE SAFETY
Once in an officer's custody, the safety of the detainee is paramount.
The detaining officer(s) shall exercise the utmost precaution to keep the detainee from escaping, injuring himself or others, and/or destroying any items of evidentiary value.

While in custody, if it appears that an officer is mistreating or abusing a detainee, or ignoring an obvious need for medical treatment, any witnessing officer(s) shall attempt to intervene in order to safeguard the detainee.

blocks.label: (a)
blocks.text: The intervening officer shall report the actions observed as soon as practical to his immediate supervisor, no later than the end of his tour.

blocks.label: (b)
blocks.text: The sworn supervisor shall determine whether a written report is necessary, and if so, shall order the officers involved to submit one. The sworn supervisor shall be responsible for forwarding the report and his observations immediately to his commander.

blocks.label: (c)
blocks.text: The commander, upon completion of his review, shall forward the report through the chain of command to the chief of police.
TRANSFER OF CUSTODY TO LCCC

A detainee remains the responsibility of the transporting officer until the actual initiation of the booking process (i.e., LCCC personnel begin the search or booking process). At that point, the custody of the detainee transfers to the LCCC.
Once custody is transferred, LCCC personnel have full responsibility and authority over the detainee.
Officers shall remain with the detainee until released by LCCC personnel, or until the detainee is secured, whichever occurs first.
Officers shall lend all appropriate assistance during the booking process.
Should an injury, which occurred prior to the initiation of the booking process, be discovered during the booking process, LCCC personnel may refuse to accept custody of the detainee.
BOOKING INFORMATION
It is imperative that the proper charges be recorded at the time of booking. It shall be the responsibility of the arresting officers to provide the transporting officers with:
The name of the detainee (if available).
The charges to be booked on, as well as the appropriate code numbers.
The name and ID number of the arresting officer.
Officers filing additional charges or changing the original on-view charges shall notify LCCC booking desk personnel of the changes.
TRANSPORTING DETAINEES TO A DETENTION FACILITY
When an officer transports a detainee to a detention facility, he shall follow the procedures and guidelines of the facility, including:
Securing firearms and other weapons, if required, before entering the facility.
Completing all documentation required by the facility (e.g., warrants, attachments).
Delivering all documentation (e.g., medical after-care instructions, attachments, warrants) and property that accompanies the detainee to the facility accepting custody of the detainee.

Following the receiving facility's procedures and guidelines for removal of the detainee’s restraints during the exchange of custody; this should normally occur with the initiation of the booking process or just prior to placing the person in a cell.
Providing additional information the receiving facility would need that is not included in other documentation (e.g., suicide risk, security risk, medical conditions).
Arresting officers shall document the detainee transaction on a CRIME REPORT (e.g., booking number, date and time of arrest, property disposition).

If a unit other than the arresting unit transports a detainee and circumstances arise during the transportation that require documentation, the transporting unit shall complete a SUPPLEMENTAL CRIME REPORT. These circumstances include but are not limited to:
Discovery of evidence, weapons, or contraband during transport or booking.
Injury to or illness of the detainee during transport or booking.
Instances where transporting officers use physical control techniques, which require an ACTION – RESPONSE REPORT (TPD FORM 29.3).
Disposition of the detainee’s property to a location other than the detention facility by the transporting unit.
TRANSPORTATION DOCUMENTATION
A CRIME REPORT/INCIDENT REPORT shall be completed by the arresting and/or reporting unit whenever a detainee is transported to a police, medical or detention facility, or to an outside police agency.

If another unit transports the detainee, the arresting/reporting unit shall record the transporting unit’s number and the officers’ names on the original report. However, if circumstances arise during the transportation that requires documentation, the transporting unit shall complete a SUPPLEMENTAL CRIME REPORT.
IN CUSTODY PRISONER TRANSPORTS

Whenever an officer removes a detainee from the custody of a detention or medical facility and transports them to another location, the officer shall complete an Incident Report. The report shall be titled “In Custody/Prisoner Transport”.
The report will serve the purpose of positively identifying the detainee being transported.

The report should identify the reason for the transport, the location where the detainee is being taken to and the requestor’s information (e.g. name of investigator, outside agency). The report shall also include the final destination of the detainee (e.g taken back to original location, transported to another medical/detention facility).
A Record Bureau number is required on the report.
If the transfer is related to a prior incident/crime, the previously generated Records Section number shall be utilized on the report.
If the transfer is not related to a prior reported incident/crime, a Records Section number shall be generated and an INCIDENT REPORT completed.

If a crime occurs during transport, officers shall complete a Crime Report documenting the details of the crime. The report shall be titled “In Custody/Prisoner Transport”. All other offenses shall be documented on the report. A new Records Section number will need to be generated.
Once the transfer is complete, the completed report shall be forwarded to the Records Section.
RESTRAINING PREGNANT AND POSTPARTUM ARRESTEES

No officer or department employee, after receiving confirmation that a female is pregnant by a health-care professional, shall knowingly restrain a female who is placed under arrest or in custody of a law enforcement officer.

A pregnant or postpartum female may be restrained with handcuffs, in front, if the female presents a serious threat of physical harm to herself, others, or property, or the female presents a substantial flight or security risk.
In making a threat assessment, officers may consider the nature of the crime, criminal history, presence of weapons or current past indications of flight or violence.
Officers shall document any and all reasons when completing crime/supplemental reports.
Ankle, leg or waist shackles shall never be used.

summary: Once someone is in your custody, **their safety is paramount**, and the directive holds you strictly accountable for the search, the restraints, the transport, and the handoff. Handcuffs are mandatory on every detainee, behind the back, no exceptions for one-man versus two-man units.

The transport rules are built around two dangers: escape and positional asphyxia. Search the person, search the car before and after, radio your odometer at both ends, seat-belt them, and get a handcuffed prone subject up onto their side or seated as soon as they are controlled.

This directive also contains the duty to intervene: if another officer is mistreating a detainee or ignoring an obvious medical need, you step in and report it to your supervisor by end of tour. Pregnant arrestees confirmed by a health care professional are not restrained except in front, for a serious threat or flight risk, and never with shackles.
must: Search every detainee thoroughly before transport and remove unlawful property, weapons or dangerous instruments, anything that could facilitate escape, and evidence. If you are transporting someone else's arrest, search again yourself (1.1, 1.2)
Make a reasonable attempt to have an opposite-sex detainee searched by a same-sex officer; if none is available, search in front of a witness (1.3.1)
Radio the dispatcher with your actual odometer reading (not trip), location and destination before leaving with any detainee, and the odometer again on arrival (1.3.2, 1.3.3)
Handcuff every detainee, hands behind the back, and keep them cuffed any time you move them from a detention or medical facility to another location (2.1, 2.1.5)
If front cuffing is unavoidable because of injury or deformity, secure the cuffs to the belt or belt loop (2.1.2)
Closely monitor any handcuffed detainee lying prone, and as soon as they are controlled move them to seated or on their side with legs no closer than 90 degrees to the torso (2.3.1, 2.3.2)
Notify a sworn supervisor before transporting anyone in a hobbling device, and ride with them in the wagon, seated behind the detainee who is seated on the floor (2.1.3)
Use a patrol wagon when one is readily available, and always for disabled or special needs detainees (2.4, 2.13)
Seat-belt every detainee to the wagon bench; if their condition prevents it, the second officer rides with them and the Crime Report explains why (2.4.2d)
Ride in the internal security compartment when the detainee is prone, not belted, hobbled, hooded, sick or injured, under arrest for OVI, or the camera is down; otherwise monitor by video (2.4.2a, b)

In a sedan: detainee in the rear passenger side seat, belted, shield closed if there is no metal screen. The non-driving officer is accountable for the detainee's security whether riding front or rear left (2.5.1, 2.6)
Search the vehicle for weapons and contraband before the detainee goes in and again after they are out (2.7)
Constantly monitor any detainee in a spit hood and document its use in the Crime Report (2.8.3, 2.8.4)
On an escape, immediately radio dispatch with location, direction of flight, description, charges and safety information, then notify your supervisor and write the Crime Report (2.10)

Get sick or injured detainees care through TFRD or the nearest hospital with EMS approval, stay with them at all times including in the ambulance and at the hospital, and pass medical instructions to LCCC (2.11)
Immediately notify an Investigations Bureau supervisor (or an on-duty detective) when a felony arrestee is admitted to the hospital (2.12)
Intervene if you see an officer mistreating a detainee or ignoring an obvious need for medical care, and report it to your immediate supervisor no later than end of tour (2.14.2)

Stay with the detainee at LCCC until released by staff or the detainee is secured, and give the transporting officers the name, charges with code numbers, and arresting officer's name and ID (2.15.2, 2.16)

Write a Crime Report or Incident Report for every transport to a police, medical, detention or outside agency facility, and an Incident Report titled In Custody/Prisoner Transport whenever you move a detainee out of a detention or medical facility (2.18, 2.19)
Document every reason for restraining a confirmed pregnant or postpartum arrestee in your reports (2.20.3)
never: Handcuff in front (absent deformity or injury), use cuffs as a come-along, or cuff a detainee to yourself (2.1.1)
Hog-tie: shackle hands to ankles, or hobble the feet with a restraint secured behind the back (2.1.4)
Transport a handcuffed detainee prone except as a last resort to keep them from hurting themselves or you (2.3.3)
Put a detainee in the front seat of any sedan, or in a wagon compartment holding police equipment or personal belongings (2.4.2c, 2.5.1a)
Leave a detainee unattended in a wagon or sedan unless a life-threatening emergency forces you to act (2.8)
Use a spit hood on anyone in respiratory distress, vomiting, needing medical attention or unconscious, or for any reason other than spitting or threatening to spit (2.8.1, 2.8.2)
Stop en route to let a detainee talk to family, friends or an attorney; that waits for a secure location (2.9)
Rely on a wheelchair as a restraint; not everyone in one is immobile (2.13.1, 2.13.2)

Knowingly restrain a female confirmed pregnant by a health care professional, except handcuffs in front for a serious threat of harm or a substantial flight or security risk; ankle, leg and waist shackles are never used (2.20)
Allow hospital visitation without the yellow copy of a Hospital Visitation Pass or Clergy pass plus valid state photo ID, with the name matching (2.12.6)
notes: Custody transfers to LCCC when their staff begin the search or booking, not when you pull in. LCCC may refuse a detainee with an injury that predates booking (2.15, 2.15.4)
A misdemeanor-only arrestee held for prolonged treatment or admitted to the hospital gets a summons (2.11.5)
A physician can ask you to remove cuffs for treatment and you may, but escape prevention stays on you (2.11.4)

Hospital guard duty: stay continuously, monitor all contacts, watch for suicide, escape and assault, search and restrain before moves within the hospital, shifts no longer than eight hours. Visits are limited to clergy, attorneys and immediate family, one at a time, two visitors a day (clergy excluded), 30 minutes max, all subject to pat down. Imminent death: call an Investigations Bureau supervisor immediately (2.12.3, 2.12.6)
A one-man unit that feels unsafe transporting one or more detainees calls dispatch for help; multiple detainees in a one-man unit is discouraged (2.5.2, 2.6.3)

Transporting units that are not the arresting unit write a Supplemental Crime Report if anything happens: contraband found, injury or illness, physical control requiring an Action Response Report, or property dropped somewhere other than the jail (2.17.7)
An investigator may uncuff a detainee in an interview room if it will help cooperation (2.1.6)
Postpartum means up to six weeks after childbirth, miscarriage or termination (Definitions)

blocks.text: Policy

One of the most basic services of a police agency is to investigate crimes that have occurred within its jurisdiction. Employees of the department shall conduct timely preliminary investigations to enhance follow-up investigative efforts and increase chances for criminal apprehension and prosecution.
Procedures
MAJOR CRIME SCENES
Upon arrival at the scene of any major crime, officers shall not touch or move anything of evidentiary nature unless there is a reason to do so.
Whenever possible, the first department member to touch any evidence should be the person with the responsibility for documentation, collection and preservation of such evidence.
The transfer of custody of physical evidence must be documented in either a crime or supplemental report and must include the following:
Date and time of transfer.
Receiving person's name and functional responsibility.
Reason for the transfer.
FIRST OFFICERS AT THE SCENE
The first officers at a major crime scene, regardless of rank or assignment, shall:
Attend to the safety of any victims or injured persons.
Secure the scene to protect evidence.
Identify and locate the perpetrator and/or witnesses.
Officers shall keep all unauthorized personnel from the scene and any other location where their presence could hinder the collection of evidence.

blocks.label: (a)
blocks.text: Police personnel at the scene should be kept to a minimum, as circumstances dictate.
Advise the dispatcher of the type of crime, suspect and/or suspect vehicle descriptions, direction of flight and weapons involved.

blocks.label: (a)
blocks.text: When it is believed the suspect may travel to another area other than the covered talk-group, the officer shall ask for crossover. If crossover is not available, the appropriate dispatchers shall transmit the information on their talk-groups as soon as possible.
Personnel completing a CRIME REPORT (TPD FORM 38.1) shall be responsible for contacting the Records Section in a timely fashion and providing information necessary for a broadcast.
Upon receipt of the information, Records Section personnel shall prepare a broadcast and have it transmitted through the NORIS computer network.
Copies of the broadcast shall be distributed as necessary to be included in the roll call information.
PRELIMINARY AND FOLLOW-UP INVESTIGATIONS
ACCOUNTABILITY

Generally, uniformed officers shall be responsible for conducting appropriate preliminary investigations of all assigned or discovered crimes occurring within the jurisdiction of the city of Toledo. In many cases, patrol officers may satisfactorily complete and conclude a case based on their initial investigation. In other cases it may be necessary to contact a supervisor and/or investigator to determine how to proceed.
CONDUCTING PRELIMINARY AND FOLLOW-UP INVESTIGATIONS
Officers conducting preliminary investigations will follow these guidelines, when appropriate, depending on the nature of the complaint:
Shall thoroughly evaluate the scene to determine if there is any evidence that would indicate a crime has been committed.

Make observations relative to all conditions and events, which pertain to the incident. These include conditions such as weather, time of day, actions of the complainant and witnesses and any other condition that may be apparent initially, but would not be apparent later.
Locate and identify witnesses, obtaining their name, address, phone number (home and work), date of birth, social security number, etc.
Protect the crime scene from being disturbed until it is processed and protect evidence.

Conduct an initial interview of the complainant and witness(s). Once uniform officers complete the preliminary investigation, it may be assigned to either the Investigations Bureau or Operations Division for follow-up, depending on the case.
RECOMMENDING FOLLOW-UP INVESTIGATION
Officers shall recommend that a follow-up investigation be conducted when they believe suspects can be identified. Officers should also recommend a follow-up investigation if:
Any arrest is made
There is a suspect
There is a witness
A suspect vehicle is observed
Any firearm is taken
The suspect causes injury
Property can be traced
There is substantial loss

Physical evidence is present When an officer recommends a follow-up, he shall check the appropriate box of the Crime Report form and state the reasons for his recommendation in the narrative portion of the report. The final determination on all follow-up investigative assignments shall rest with the Investigations supervisor.
RESPONSIBILITIES OF UNIFORMED COMMAND OFFICERS
The ranking Operations command officer at the scene shall have overall control and accountability for any tactical situation and all department personnel at the scene.
The ranking Operations command officer shall maintain such control and accountability until the tactical situation is concluded or he is properly relieved.
INVESTIGATIVE RESPONSIBILITY

The ranking investigator at the scene shall take exclusive control of the crime scene in matters pertaining to the investigation, and shall be responsible for the conduct of all phases of the investigation.
The concerned investigator or specialist shall assume command of the crime scene by identifying himself and informing the officer then in command.
The Investigations Bureau supervisor shall be notified as soon as practicable in the following cases:
Cases of violent death.
Financial institution robberies.
Any event in which an officer is involved in a shooting.
It shall be the responsibility of the ranking investigator at the scene to ensure these notifications are made.
MAJOR CRIME SCENE PERSONNEL LOG
Upon arrival at major crime scenes, the Operations supervisor shall designate an officer to maintain the MAJOR CRIME SCENE PERSONNEL LOG (TPD FORM 31.16).
This officer shall be posted where he can monitor who enters and leaves the crime scene.
The log shall be completed accurately and completely.

When on-scene operations are complete, the log shall be turned directly over to the investigator in charge who shall ensure officers who were present at the crime scene prepare a SUPPLEMENTAL REPORT (TPD FORM 38.3).
REPORTS
The Operations command officer in charge of the overall situation shall designate the police unit responsible for completing the initial CRIME REPORT.

If the command officer or ranking investigator so determines, he shall instruct all police personnel at the scene, or those who have had any connection with the incident, to complete a SUPPLEMENTAL REPORT to include their actions and observation.
HOMICIDE CRIME SCENE PROTECTION TAPE
When an officer at the crime scene has determined the incident is a homicide, a shift sergeant shall be notified of the situation.
The shift sergeant shall determine if and how the scene needs to be protected.
The shift sergeant may utilize department-issued crime scene tape.

Once a scene has been cordoned off with tape, no one, including any police personnel, regardless of rank, shall be allowed into the crime scene area without permission from the investigator in charge or the Coroner’s Assistant at the scene.
PHOTOGRAPHIC IDENTIFICATIONS, USE OF PHOTOS

The showing of photographs for suspect identification purposes shall be the responsibility of Investigations Bureau personnel when conducting follow-up investigations. Operations personnel shall not conduct photographic identifications of suspects.

ISB officers conducting follow-up investigations may show a photo array that includes a suspect; however, the photographic identification procedure must conform to all ISD procedures. The array must not be “suggestive” or “fundamentally unfair”.
At no time shall any officer who is conducting an investigation into an offense show only one or two photographs of potential suspects to a witness or victim.

NOTE: Nothing in this order prevents Field Operations personnel, or other officers, engaged in locating “wanted persons” from using a single photograph of a person wanted on an existing arrest warrant. In these incidents, a single photograph may be shown to neighbors or coworkers to positively identify and/or aid in locating a suspect.
Policy

Information gathering is a fundamental and essential element in the all-encompassing duties of any law enforcement agency. When acquired, information is used to prevent crime, pursue and apprehend offenders, and obtain evidence necessary for conviction. It is the policy of the Toledo Police Department to gather information directed toward specific individuals or organizations where there is reasonable suspicion that said individuals or organizations may be planning or engaging in criminal activity. Intelligence will be gathered with due respect for the privacy and constitutional rights of those involved and disseminated only to authorized individuals. All members of the Toledo Police Department shall be responsible for reporting information that may help identify criminal conspirators and perpetrators.
Definitions

any files where the investigation has been completed, all logical leads have been exhausted, or where no legitimate law enforcement interest exists. CONFIDENTIAL INTELLIGENCE FILES – files containing information that is less sensitive than restricted files, but requires demonstration of need-to-know basis. CRIMINAL INTELLIGENCE – information compiled, analyzed, and/or disseminated in an effort to anticipate, prevent, or monitor criminal activity. INTELLIGENCE CYCLE – the process of developing raw information into finished intelligence through the five steps of: planning and direction, collection, processing, analysis and production, and dissemination. OPEN INTELLIGENCE FILE – any case being actively investigated. RESTRICTED INTELLIGENCE FILES – files containing information that could adversely affect an investigation, create safety hazards for or identify officers, informants, or other individuals. SPECIAL INTELLIGENCE GROUP – reports directly to the Commander of the Special Investigations Section.
