Additionally, if the suspect caused serious injury or death to another person, the OVI may become an element of a more serious charge, such as Aggravated Vehicular Assault, or Aggravated Vehicular Homicide, if OVI is not charged. To ensure that test results are admissible in court, the following procedure shall be used whenever an individual is involved in a serious injury or fatal accident, and is not being placed under arrest. The accident investigator shall not read the back of the ADMINISTRATIVE LICENSE SUSPENSION FORM, BMV 2255 to the suspect.

The individual shall be asked to voluntarily submit to a blood, breath, or urine test. The WAIVER OF SEARCH WARRANT BLOOD, BREATH OR URINE SAMPLE (TPD FORM 17.23), shall be filled out and signed, if consent is given.
If the individual refuses, the assigned accident reconstructionist shall proceed by search warrant to secure any blood or urine samples taken at the medical facility by staff.

If blood or urine samples are not taken by the medical facility, the assigned accident reconstructionist shall proceed by search warrant to secure a blood sample from the individual, by following the established procedure.
REMOVED
OVI/SOL UNIT
The OVI/SOL Unit shall be responsible for conducting and processing investigations concerning OVI’s, Felony OVI’s, SOL’s, and Wrongful Entrustment cases.
ALCOHOL ENFORCEMENT COUNTERMEASURES

Alcohol enforcement countermeasures are additional enforcement techniques that generally go beyond normal traffic enforcement duties. The Traffic Section has the primary responsibility for conducting alcohol enforcement countermeasures. The Traffic Section commander shall analyze crash data and OVI arrest reports to determine where, when, and how alcohol countermeasures are to be employed. Summaries of OVI arrest reports will be provided to the Operations Division for use by district units while they are on patrol.
Policy

Officers encounter a variety of situations when it is necessary to tow a motor vehicle, trailer, recreational/off-road vehicle or other vehicles by either impoundment or movement to an alternate location. Liability and responsibility exists when towing a vehicle so as not to release a vehicle to unauthorized individuals.
Definitions
Heavy-duty tows are used for larger sized commercial vehicles.

IMPOUND TOW − All police ordered tows are impound tows, and shall be taken to the Toledo Police Department Impound Lot unless directed by the Records Section Auto Desk clerk to take the vehicle to another location. PRIVATE TOW – Private tows are made when there is no investigatory or regulatory reason to impound the vehicle and the owner has requested assistance in obtaining a towing service. Private tows do not require an IMPOUND REPORT (TPD FORM 63.1) and the city tow list rotation does not apply. HOLDER – A special status applied to (or removed from) an impounded vehicle by an investigator or command officer that prohibits the release of a motor vehicle or other property until specific requirements are met. This includes hit-skip accidents and OVI/SOL situations.
AutoReturn Integrated Enterprise System; a flexible component-based system that manages the entire lifecycle of a tow and provides comprehensive reporting.
Digital tow request using the ARIES Request shortcut on the Mobile Data Computer (MDC).
Cloud-based electronic dispatch and towing management system.
The electronic inventory management, receipt generation, and payment processing system for administering impound activities.
Web-based tow file vehicle search.
Procedures
TOWING
WHEN TOW SERVICE IS REQUIRED
An officer shall use an authorized police towing service for removal of any of the following:
Automobiles, vans, trucks, motor homes and buses
Motorcycles, and gasoline motor-driven cycles
Off-highway vehicles, including racing vehicles, construction equipment, dune buggies, all-terrain vehicles, snowmobiles, riding lawn mowers and tractors
Trailers (all types)
Boats
Any item too large to carry (e.g. a safe, etc.)
OBTAINING TOW SERVICE

Prior to towing any vehicle, an officer shall check the vehicle identification number (VIN) and license number through LEADS and NCIC for registration (ownership), stolen/wanted, attempt to locate (ATL), parking tickets, etc. The VIN shall be obtained through actual visual inspection of the VIN plate.

Officers will query the vehicle through the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) to ensure the vehicle is not stolen, etc.; however, officers shall not use the information obtained through LEADS/NCIC/NORIS/LexisNexus/Accurint for entry into ARIES. Officers will visually verify the make, model and vehicle license number, dashboard VIN number plate, and the VIN sticker on the inner door frame (door itself, A-pillar, or glovebox). The towing officer will request the tow operator unlock vehicles to enable verification of both VIN data plates and conduct the required inventory search.
All requests for tow service shall be made through the AUTURA/ARIES.
An officer requesting a tow shall provide the following information:
Unit number
Employee I.D. number
Location of the vehicle
Make, model and color of the vehicle
License and VIN
If keys are left with tow operator
If equipped with radio
Reason for tow
RESPONSIBILITIES AND TYPES OF TOWS
REPORTING TOWED VEHICLES

Officers towing a vehicle shall complete an ARIES/Request for each vehicle towed. All appropriate boxes shall be completed, including the VIN which shall be obtained through visual inspection of the vehicle, time of tow and any damage or unusual features (e.g. mismatched tires)

If the vehicle is towed in connection with an incident reported on a CRIME REPORT (TPD FORM 38.1) or INCIDENT REPORT (TPD FORM 38.12), the Records Section number of the incident shall also be listed in the designated field in ARIES.
If a tow violation occurs, it shall be noted in the notes field in ARIES.
ASSIGNMENT OF TOWS
An officer at a scene where multiple tows have been ordered shall be responsible for assigning the correct towing firm as determined by the ARIES/AutoReturn.
If multiple tows are requested in ARIES the assignment of tow trucks will be done automatically by the program.
KEYS AND REGISTRATION CERTIFICATE IN A TOWED VEHICLE

If a properly identified owner is at the scene, he may be permitted to remove the registration certificate from an impounded vehicle for later release of his vehicle from the Impound Lot. The registration certificate shall not be removed from a towed vehicle by an officer unless it is booked as evidence and so noted on the IMPOUND REPORT.

Officers shall obtain ignition keys, trunk keys and vehicle keyless entry remotes when available and give them to the tow truck operator. Windows, doors, trunks and sunroofs shall also be closed when possible.
MANDATORY IMPOUND TOW
Officers shall impound vehicles if they fall into any one of the following categories:
Abandoned and/or traffic hazard.
Altered/missing or unverified Vehicle Identification Number (VIN).

If the VIN cannot be verified, or has been altered or removed, the Records Section Auto Desk and the Investigations Bureau shall be notified so that a holder may be placed on the vehicle for the Auto Unit.
In addition to the IMPOUND REPORT, a CRIME REPORT shall be completed detailing the circumstances.
Driver is arrested for Operating a Vehicle While Under Influence (OVI) AND has a prior OVI conviction.
Driver has a court ordered suspension, OVI suspension or an FRA suspension.
Delinquent Parking Tags – Vehicle must have two or more delinquent tags and be in violation of a parking ordinance at the time of the tow.
The Records Section shall verify the delinquent tags through ParkSmart before the vehicle may be towed.
Officers shall tag the vehicle for the immediate violation.
Legally parked vehicles, or vehicles being operated, may not be towed for delinquent parking tickets.
Any vehicle held for evidence.
Removed
Hit-Skip Vehicles – Officers shall tow a vehicle that was involved in a hit-skip accident if the driver has fled the scene.
The investigating officers shall place a holder for hit-skip on the vehicle by Placing the appropriate holder within ARIES.
Illegally Parked Vehicles – A parking ticket shall be issued to an illegally parked vehicle prior to it being towed. An officer may tow an illegally parked vehicle when it:
Obstructs the normal movement of traffic.
Is left upon a street, highway, bridge, viaduct, railroad tracks, underpass or alley.
Is impractical to move the vehicle to a legal parking place in the near vicinity.
Recovered stolen auto – Owner cannot be notified (See Directive 406.3/3.1 TOWING RECOVERED STOLEN VEHICLES).
Tampered vehicle – Probable stolen; supervisor's approval needed. (See Directive 406.3/3.2 RECOVERING TAMPERED VEHICLES).
Vehicles involved in fatal or serious injury accidents.
HEAVY-DUTY TOW
To request a heavy-duty tow service, officers shall select heavy duty tow in ARIES.
PRIVATE TOW

A private tow shall be ordered only upon the request of the verified owner (or spouse) of the vehicle, when the vehicle is properly insured, and when there is no investigatory or regulatory reason to impound the vehicle.
The owner may state his preference of tow company and shall arrange with the tow operator where the vehicle is to be taken.
An IMPOUND REPORT is not required for a private tow.
Once a police impound tow is ordered though ARIES, it shall not be changed to a private tow.
STOLEN OR TAMPERED VEHICLES
TOWING RECOVERED STOLEN VEHICLES
When an officer recovers a stolen vehicle and the owner or his agent cannot be promptly notified to take possession of the vehicle, the officer shall impound the vehicle.
Officers observing damage that may affect a vehicle's operability shall note this in the appropriate section in ARIES.
Officers shall carefully check recovered vehicles for property or other evidence.
In addition to the ARIES REQUEST, a CRIME REPORT shall be completed entitled ‘Recovered Stolen Auto.
RECOVERING TAMPERED VEHICLES
Some vehicles are recovered before the owner discovers the vehicle has been stolen.

Officers finding a vehicle that appears to have been stolen, but has not yet been reported, shall notify the Records Section to attempt to notify the owner. If the owner cannot be notified, officers shall notify a command officer to request the vehicle be impounded for safekeeping.
In addition to the ARIES/REQUEST, a CRIME REPORT shall be completed entitled, “Theft of a Motor Vehicle”, and indicating “Attempted” from the drop down menu.
VEHICLE PROPERTY INVENTORY
RESPONSIBILITY FOR ARRESTEE'S VEHICLE
Arresting officers shall exercise reasonable care of a vehicle taken from the immediate physical possession of an arrestee.
PROPERTY IN VEHICLE
When a vehicle is either towed or left legally parked at the scene following a police incident, the following items shall be removed and booked in accordance with established procedures:
All property of evidentiary value, whether in plain sight or found as the result of a search or inventory.
Property in plain sight that is estimated by the officer to be of value, when these items cannot be locked in the glove box or trunk.
Any items of evidentiary value in the trunk or glove box of the vehicle that come into the sight of officers securing property from the driver's compartment.
All monies found, whether in plain sight or as a result of a search.
Any item declared to be of value by the person in apparent lawful control of the vehicle.

All property, whether in plain sight or found as a result of a search or inventory, which is left in a towed vehicle, shall be listed on the IMPOUND REPORT. If needed, a SUPPLEMENTAL CRIME REPORT (TPD FORM 38.3) listing additional property shall be completed and attached to the IMPOUND REPORT.
PROPERTY IN LOCKED COMPARTMENTS AND CLOSED CONTAINERS
The towing officer shall inventory all locked compartments within the towed vehicle if keys to said compartments are readily available.
If keys are not available, the locked compartment shall be noted on the IMPOUND REPORT and not forced open as part of a normal inventory.
When searching for specific evidence officers shall be guided by legal procedures, such as obtaining a search warrant, applicable to each specific case.
The towing officer shall inventory the contents of all closed containers (i.e., boxes, bags or unlocked suitcases), prior to locking them in the trunk.
Officers shall not open locked containers, but shall list them on the vehicle inventory.
Any container booked into the Property Room or Night Property Rooms shall be opened for safety purposes.
OTHER TOWING PROCEDURES
TOWING FROM CITY-OWNED LOTS
An officer may impound a vehicle that is parked in a municipal parking lot without proper authorization.

Vehicles parked in metered lots shall not be towed for overtime parking unless they create a traffic obstruction or hazard; however, vehicles parked in positions which aggravate conditions in the lot (i.e., blocking aisles or driveways, etc.) should be tagged and impounded.
Where permits have been authorized and issued to limit parking, private vehicles not bearing the appropriate permit should be tagged and may be impounded.
REPORTING OF PRIVATE PERSON TOWS OR REPOSSESSIONS

When a private person notifies the department that he intends to cause the removal of a vehicle from private property for parking on the property or as a repossession, the officer receiving the notification shall direct the person to the Records Section.
Employees in the Records Section shall ensure vehicles that have been privately towed are logged as third party tows so they are not reported as stolen at a later time.
Police towing permittees are required to notify the Records Section of the identification of all vehicles privately towed by them without notice to the owner.

If the vehicle is obstructing driveways, loading docks, ingress, or egress, try to locate the owner and have the vehicle moved immediately. If unable to locate the owner, impound the vehicle. Include a brief investigative summary and the property owner’s name who requested the vehicle removed in the ARIES/Request driver’s notes.
SPECIAL EVENTS
Instructions for towing illegally parked vehicles in the vicinity of a special event shall be given prior to the event.
SNOW EMERGENCIES
Instructions for towing vehicles during a snow emergency shall be given to personnel participating in their removal.
VEHICLE NOT TO BE CONFISCATED FOR FEDERAL VIOLATION

A vehicle in which there has been transported, or in which there is found, contraband drugs, gambling equipment or illegal weapons, in violation of federal statutes, may be confiscated by the appropriate federal agency. Officers may not seize and tow a vehicle for the sole purpose of facilitating its later confiscation by federal authorities.
WHEN NOT TO TOW A VEHICLE

If, at any time, a vehicle which is improperly or illegally parked so as to create a traffic obstruction and is attended by the lawful owner or his agent, the owner is responsible for the removal of the vehicle, unless he is placed in custody.

No officer shall tow a vehicle when the owner is capable of promptly caring for it himself or grants some other responsible person the accountability for its care, absent justification as the listed in Directive 406.3/2.3 – MANDATORY IMPOUND TOW.
Should the owner or his agent neglect or refuse to remove the vehicle promptly, officers may tow it after 15 minutes, if they have previously ordered it removed.
CANCELLATION OF TOW – OWNER NOW PRESENT
Release vehicles not needed for evidence or by other authorities, to persons with right of possession if they are at the scene before the tow truck operator has arrived.
Complete the ARIES/Request entry. Write “Released to Owner” in the driver’s notes.
Cancel the tow in ARIES/Request to put the tow company back on top of the rotation list.

If the tow company arranges to tow the vehicle to an address other than the Impound Lot, contact the Auto Desk and advise them the vehicle needs to be placed in a “not stored status”. The tow should not be cancelled. Tow operators do not have authority to cancel a tow.
HOLDERS ON TOWED VEHICLES
PLACING A HOLDER ON A VEHICLE
A notation shall be made in both the CRIME REPORT and ARIES indicating that a holder was placed on the vehicle.
The tow truck operator shall be cautioned if there is danger of destroying or contaminating evidence.

To place a holder on a vehicle, the authorizing investigator's or command officer's name and I.D. number are required. EXCEPTIONS – Patrol officers are authorized to place holders on vehicles involved in hit-skip accidents when the driver has not been identified and in OVI/SOL incidents.
INVESTIGATOR TO CONFIRM HOLDER OR RELEASE VEHICLE
When an investigating officer is assigned a case involving an impounded vehicle, he shall promptly make all necessary arrangements for searching or collecting evidence as may be required.
The assigned investigator shall ensure that the vehicle holder is removed as soon as practical by completing the ‘Release of Investigation Holder on Impound Vehicle’ located on the TPD Intranet.
If an extended examination of the impounded vehicle is needed, the investigator shall confirm the holder with the Impound Lot.
NOTIFICATION TO OWNER OF IMPOUNDED VEHICLE
When a vehicle is impounded, the Impound Lot shall ensure that written notification is made to the owner of the impounded vehicle.
When a vehicle previously held for investigation is available for release, the investigating officer shall immediately notify the Impound Lot and make notification to the owner.
FINGERPRINTS ON IMPOUNDED VEHICLE

Whenever possible, officers shall process fingerprints and/or other evidence within a vehicle at the scene before ordering the tow. If it becomes necessary to impound the vehicle, the impounding officer shall:
Seek authorization from the concerned investigative officer.
Notify Records Section Auto Desk that an investigative tow is needed.
List in the IMPOUND REPORT the name of the person who was notified of the vehicle being held for prints.
Notify the tow truck operator that the vehicle is to be held for prints and stored inside.
Escort the tow truck operator to the location for inside storage as directed by the Auto Desk.
TOWING VICTIM'S VEHICLE FOR EVIDENCE COLLECTION
On occasion, a victim's vehicle is ordered towed for the purpose of processing evidence.

The department shall pay towing and storage fees when the vehicle is in the property of, or lawfully used by, a victim of a crime and such vehicle has been ordered towed and held by the department for evidentiary processing.
Where practical, processing of vehicles for evidence should be done at the scene.
If a vehicle needs to be washed due to the processing of the vehicle for evidence, the cleaning shall be completed at a city-contracted car wash.
The final determination of payment shall be made by the commander of the Records Section.
TOW OPERATORS
REGULATION OF TOWING OPERATIONS

Officers shall notify the Records Section commander, by completing a SUPERVISOR’S REPORT (TPD FORM 20.7), of all violations of ordinances, which regulate towing operations within the city. The Records Section commander shall investigate and, if warranted, forward his recommendations on revocation or suspension of police towing permits to the Deputy Chief of Staff/Safety Director.
VIOLATIONS BY PERMITTEES

When an officer observes a violation of any towing ordinance (TMC Chapter 765) by a towing firm licensed by the city to tow vehicles for the department, or when such permittee violates any law and no other reports are prepared, or when an officer observes any incident where notification is deemed desirable:

He shall complete a SUPERVISOR'S REPORT describing the circumstance and forward it to the Records Section commander. The report shall contain information sufficient to fully identify the driver, the vehicle and the towing firm.
When a violation of the towing ordinance is aggravated, an officer may complete a citation in lieu of the SUPERVISOR'S REPORT.
When a citation is issued to a permitee, the officer shall forward a photocopy of the citation to the Records Section commander.
Additional comments shall be added to the photocopy to explain the circumstances of the violation.
CLEARING DEBRIS FROM AN ACCIDENT

The officer in charge of the accident investigation shall instruct the tow truck operator when he may remove all broken glass and other debris from the street at the scene of the accident. Failure to remove all glass, metal, plastic or vehicle parts is a violation of TMC Section 765.11(c) and shall be reported to the Records Section commander in writing.
ABANDONED OR JUNK VEHICLES
JUNK VEHICLE
When a vehicle has been abandoned on private property for 72 hours or longer, or on a public trafficway for 48 hours or longer, it may be classified as junk, if it is:
Three years old, or older, and,
Extensively damaged (missing wheels, motor, tires, transmission, etc.)
It is apparent that it is inoperable, and worth less than $1500
Officers shall report all junk vehicles to the Traffic Section by preparing an INCIDENT REPORT entitled, ‘Junk Vehicle.’
ABANDONED OR JUNK VEHICLES ON PRIVATE PROPERTY
When a person is adversely affected by an abandoned vehicle, an officer at the scene shall make a preliminary investigation to determine if the vehicle has actually been abandoned.
A vehicle is considered to be abandoned if it is inoperable and a public nuisance, as stated in TMC 521.09.

The officer shall check the license and VIN with the Records Section and shall submit an INCIDENT REPORT entitled 'Abandoned Vehicle – Private Property' which shall be forwarded to the Traffic Section.
The report shall contain:
Name and address of complainant
Name and address of person having control of the property
A statement indicating that the person having control of the property did not give express or implied consent to any person to park or leave this vehicle on this property, if applicable
Name and address of the registered owner of the vehicle, if available
Description of the vehicle, its condition, license number and the VIN
In the case of a blocked driveway on private property, the officer should advise the property owner that he may arrange for towing the vehicle away.
ABANDONED VEHICLES ON PUBLIC PROPERTY
When a vehicle has apparently been abandoned on public property (e.g. a park), officers shall first determine if the vehicle has been reported stolen.
If not stolen, mark around the tires on the pavement and on subsequent days, tag it for overtime parking if it remains in the same location.
After 48 hours the vehicle may be impounded and towed if it has not been driven.
If the vehicle has two or more outstanding delinquent tags, it may be towed. It is not necessary to wait 48 hours.
DISPOSITION OF ABANDONED AND JUNK VEHICLES

The Traffic Section shall conduct a follow-up investigation on the condition and status of all abandoned and junk vehicles, whether the complaint was received from a citizen, from Communications, or from an officer. The Records Section shall determine ownership, make a written notification, photograph junk vehicles and prepare the necessary affidavits to comply with state and municipal laws on the disposition of such vehicles, by scrapping or sale at public auction.
NON-EMEREGENCY ACCESS AUTHORIZATION

Department members receiving a request for assistance in entering a locked vehicle, or building, absent any emergency or exigent circumstances, shall advise the complainant that there is the possibility of damage during the entry attempt. The person requesting assistance will be required to sign a TOLEDO POLICE ACCESS AUTHORIZATION (T.P.D. FORM 15.6) that releases the Department from any liability. Officers shall also ascertain that the person requesting the access has legitimate authority to do so. Officers shall complete any other required reports based on the nature of the incident and forward copies of the TOLEDO POLICE ACCESS AUTHORIZATION form as indicated on the form.
Policy

It shall be the policy of the Toledo Police Department to establish guidelines regarding instrument checks for evidential breath testing equipment. This policy shall also provide guidelines for requiring sworn officers to maintain an active BAC Intoxilyzer Operator Breath Testing Permit. This policy shall establish specific instrument checks, operation, and repair documentation guidelines for the I-8000 INTOXILYZER breath testing machines.
Procedures
BREATH TESTING PERMITS
SENIOR OPERATOR IN CHARGE

The Operations Division Commander shall designate a 1-8000 Intoxilyzer Operator to be the Senior Operator in Charge (SOIC) of all evidential breath testing equipment assigned to the department. The SOIC is the point of contact for the Ohio Department of Health (ODH), Bureau of Drug and Alcohol Testing and their inspectors who are responsible for scheduling, testing and training all sworn operators of the I-8000 Intoxilyzer.
PERMIT RENEWAL
The Ohio Department of Health is responsible for the testing and issuance of all BAC Intoxilyzer Operator Breath Testing Permits.
An Operator Breath Testing Permit may be renewed any time within six months prior to its one-year expiration, by the performance of a subject breath test.
The Senior Operator in Charge (SOIC) will coordinate renewal proficiency tests at the department level.
All operators must successfully complete an annual proficiency test. Failure to pass a proficiency test for renewal will result in the loss of the Operator Permit.
All sworn personnel with Operator Breath Testing Permits shall maintain proficiency, as outlined by the Senior Operator in Charge.
Each district station shall be provided with guidelines for completing a proficiency exam.
REMOVED
I-8000 INTOXILYZER
The I-8000 INTOXILYZER evidential breath testing equipment shall be operated in accordance with:
The OHIO DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH (ODH) BUREAU OF DRUG AND ALCOHOL Testing rules and regulations, OHIO ADMINISTRATIVE CODE (OAC), CHAPTER 3701 – 53.
I-8000 Intoxilyzer operator’s manual, provided by the manufacturer.
Applicable Ohio revised code statues.
Toledo Police Department's policies, procedures, and training.
DOCUMENTATION
The (SOIC) will be responsible for maintaining all forms and special instructions pertaining to the I-8000 INTOXILYZER breath testing machines.
REMOVED
SPECIAL INSTRUCTIONS FOR FORMS
Test site number #4807. Use the Toledo Police Department's test site number, #4807, which is assigned by the OHIO DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH.
The I-8000 Intoxilyzer automatically prints two copies of the HEA2650 Form on all subjects tested. File one form in the OVI/SOL packet

File the second copy of the HEA 2650 form in the I-8000 INTOXILYZER LOG BOOK at the testing site. After 100 pages are complete, the SOIC will remove from the binder’s content and store in a secure area accessible only to departmental employees.
Security
PROCESSING AREAS
GENERAL GUIDELINES FOR USE OF A PROCESSING/TESTING AREA
The area where the alcohol breath tests are conducted are considered secured areas.
Officers shall inspect the Processing/Testing Area for weapons, contraband, or unsafe conditions prior to placing a detainee in the room/area and immediately after removing the detainee.

Prior to placing a detainee into a Processing/Testing Area, officers shall remove all property from the detainee. The property shall be placed in one (1) of the property lockers provided near the Processing Area. Officers shall secure the locker and maintain possession of the property locker key until the property transfers with the detainee.

Weapons, contraband or evidence shall be handled in accordance with existing procedures. All other property shall transfer with the detainee when they are transported to another facility or released from custody.

While in a Processing/Testing Area, all detainees shall be handcuffed to a handcuff detainment device to ensure detainee safety, officer safety, prevent escape, and to prevent damage to the Processing/Testing Area, if applicable.

The proper handcuffing technique to secure a detainee to a handcuff detention device is both hands handcuffed together behind the back with the operable portion of the handcuff detention device attached around the chain or hinge portion of the detainee’s handcuffs.
If no detention device is available, officers shall ensure that both of the detainee’s hands remain handcuffed behind the back.
The handcuffs may be removed from the detainee to conduct the required breath tests.

Once the tests have been concluded, the detainee shall be removed from the Processing/Testing Area and relocated to the Temporary Detention Area and secured per DM 306.1, while the officer completes required paperwork.
While a detainee is in the Processing Area, the officer shall keep the detainee under continual supervision.
SECURITY MEASURES

Officers shall secure all firearms before entering a Processing Area with a detainee, or before entering a Processing Area that contains a detainee. Officers shall secure their firearms in one (1) of the gun lockers installed outside the Processing Area entrance. Officers should also consider securing other potentially harmful weapons prior to entering a Processing Area.
Officers may utilize a duress alarm or the emergency button on a portable radio to summon assistance.

Only authorized personnel (e.g., police personnel) shall be permitted in Processing Areas or to have access to detainees. Other individuals, such as attorneys and family members, will have access to a detainee after the detainee is booked into a permanent detention facility.

Officers shall allow reasonable water and restroom breaks for their detainees. Officers shall keep in mind the circumstances, the length of the temporary detention, and any security risk involved in removing handcuffs to allow a detainee to use restroom facilities. If there is any doubt on the part of the officer, a sworn supervisor or investigator shall decide what action to take.

blocks.label: (a)
blocks.text: When a detainee is granted permission to use restroom facilities, an officer shall search the restroom for weapons, evidence or contraband before and after escorting the detainee to the restroom. The officer shall also monitor the detainee’s activities as closely as possible.

blocks.label: (b)
blocks.text: When an opposite-sex detainee is involved, a sworn supervisor shall be advised and he shall render a decision whether to summon an officer of the appropriate sex, or allow the detainee to use the restroom facilities unsupervised.
Policy

The Toledo Police Department is committed to the proper collection and preservation of physical evidence. These guidelines are written to ensure that physical evidence is identified, collected and properly preserved to protect the evidentiary integrity for possible court presentation, and when necessary, promptly conveyed to the appropriate laboratory or office for analysis to ensure its effectiveness in criminal cases.
Definitions
the computer microprocessing chip that contains several thousand to several million transistors that perform multiple functions simultaneously.

the genetic material present in the cells of all living organisms. DNA is the fundamental building block for an individual’s entire genetic makeup. A person’s DNA is the same in every cell (with a nucleus), which is inherited half from each biological parent. The DNA in a person's blood is the same as the DNA in their skin cells, semen and saliva. An individual's DNA is unique except in cases of identical twins.

information and data of value to an investigation that is stored on, received, or transmitted by an electronic device. Sources of potential digital evidence include computer systems, hard drives, removable media, thumb drives (flash drives), memory cards, handheld devices, data storage tapes, surveillance equipment, cellular telephones, personal digital assistants (PDA) and MP3 players. Digital evidence is fragile and sensitive to extreme temperatures, humidity, physical shock, static electricity, and magnetic fields.

any detective assigned to the Crime Scene Investigation Unit, which processes crime scenes for evidence, and gathers, collects, marks, protects and preserves evidence for future analysis and/or court presentation.
an impression of the friction ridges of all or any part of the finger.
an envelope used to package memory cards containing images from the department’s digital cameras and PHOTO PLACARDS (TPD FORM 25.1).
a system of connected devices that communicate and share services (several computers linked together that share common resources).
NOTE: A single computer connected to an Internet Service Provider (ISP) through a modem is not an example of a network.

computer programs (which are stored in and executed by an operating system and computer hardware) and associated data (which is also stored in the hardware) that may be dynamically written or modified during execution.
device which maintains power to the computer through powerful batteries, even after electrical power is lost.
Procedures
CRIME SCENE INVESTIGATION AND PHYSICAL EVIDENCE MANUAL
A copy of the Crime Scene Investigation Unit - Crime Scene Investigation and Physical Evidence Manual shall be available at all district stations for reference.
REQUESTING CRIME SCENE INVESTIGATION UNIT (CSIU) SERVICES

When the services of an evidence technician are needed for evidence collection, the requesting officer shall complete a CRIME SCENE INVESTIGATION UNIT– REQUEST FOR SERVICES (TPD FORM 28.8). The original form shall be forwarded to the Records Section and a copy sent to the Crime Scene Investigation Unit.
COLLECTION OF FINGERPRINTS

Fingerprint evidence remains the most positive means of identification in law enforcement. Therefore, it is imperative that officers search crime scenes for physical evidence, including fingerprint evidence.

When officers are involved in a major crime scene investigation where the Investigations Bureau and Crime Scene Investigation Unit will be responding, officers shall protect the crime scene and any potential physical evidence.
At all other crime scenes, officers are responsible for processing the scenes for fingerprints and/or other evidence, whenever possible, using the following guidelines.
Officers should use their issued fingerprint kit when processing crime scenes for fingerprints.

blocks.label: (a)
blocks.text: When officers process fingerprints, they shall transfer the fingerprint to a lift card. Officers shall label the reverse side of the card with the Records Section number, the date and time the print was lifted, the location where the print was lifted (e.g., inside window glass at point of entry), the processing officer’s initials, and his identification number. The lift card will be handled as evidence.

blocks.label: (b)
blocks.text: Items an officer feels cannot be processed at the scene will be collected, protected for prints and booked into the Property Room. If possible, officers shall package the item in a paper bag.

EXCEPTION: Motor vehicles involved in major crimes, which need to be processed by Crime Scene Investigation Unit personnel, shall be towed to the Impound Lot, and if necessary, protected in the inside storage area.

blocks.label: (c)
blocks.text: If an item is too large to be transported to the Property Room, it shall be protected at the scene.

In all instances, officers shall complete a CRIME SCENE INVESTIGATION UNIT – REQUEST FOR SERVICES, requesting the appropriate services from the Crime Scene Investigation Unit (e.g., AFIS search, process for latent prints, the location of the item and the services requested of Crime Scene Investigation Unit personnel).

All fingerprints will be entered into the Automated Fingerprint Identification System (AFIS) by Crime Scene Investigation Unit personnel. All identifications will be made by members of the Crime Scene Investigations Unit.
SEIZING COMPUTERS AND DIGITAL EVIDENCE

Computer and related devices may contain digital evidence and shall be processed in the following manner. Officer safety and the safety of everyone at the scene should be an officer’s primary consideration. Officers should be cognizant that there have been instances where computers have been booby trapped with explosive devices. Any officer who encounters a computer that appears to be tampered with shall notify the commander of the Technical Services Section for assistance.

In cases where it is necessary to seize a computer which is part of a network, or where a business is using a mainframe computer, officers shall contact the Computer Crimes Office before seizing any computer files or equipment or executing a search warrant.

Due to the expertise required in examining digital evidence and the ease with which evidence can be damaged or destroyed, officers shall use the following procedure when the seizure of a computer is necessary and Investigative Services Division personnel are not available.
In all cases involving a seized computer, officers shall not open the case containing the Central Processing Unit (CPU) without Computer Crimes Office personnel present.

Remove all individuals, especially the suspect, from the area surrounding the computer. Make sure that no one can touch the keyboard, the mouse or the CPU case, including law enforcement personnel. Officers shall not search the computer for evidence or turn the computer on or off.

Do not accept any offers of assistance in shutting down the computer or saving documents from the subject or their associates, as simple commands can be used to reprogram the computer to cause data loss or damage to the operating system.
Remove all network and phone connections from the CPU case. These connections can by used to remotely control the computer. Evidence can be deleted from a remote location.

Record any pertinent data displayed on the computer display, or monitor. Videotape or photograph the image on the screen if it is any image other than a simple screensaver. Data displayed on the computer’s monitor may not have been saved to permanent media, such as the hard disk drive and exists only in random access memory (RAM).

Disconnect the power from the CPU case by pulling the electrical cord from the CPU case. The system may be connected to an uninterruptible power supply (UPS). Computers have the ability to detect when power is lost and use the UPS to shut down, or potentially launch a malicious application.

NOTE: If information or activity onscreen indicates that data is being deleted or overwritten, or there is indication that a destructive process is being performed, the officer shall immediately disconnect power from the CPU case by pulling the electrical cord from the CPU case.

Photograph and sketch the computer’s setup. The information may be valuable to show the computer setup, or to reconstruct the computer system for examination at a later date. It is also likely that the individual examining the computer may not be the same individual that seized it and this provides a valuable visual aid to the examiner.

Seize all related documents regarding the operation of the computer. Material around the computer such as manuals, handwritten notes, printouts and postits notes may provide valuable clues concerning passwords, the operation of the software and hardware, the location and type of evidence stored on the computer and leads to other suspects.

Dismantle the computer components as little as necessary to package and transport the computer to the Property Room. Label each connector and its connecting point for easy reassembly. Mark the computer system as evidence, but do not mark the evidence where it will cause damage to the computer should the computer have to be returned to the owner.

The computer components should be secured in the back seat of the vehicle if at all possible, to protect against environmental extremes such as heat, cold, fluids, jarring impacts and other damaging conditions such as electromagnetic radiation from the radio transmitter in the trunk of police vehicles.
Officers should take all steps reasonably necessary to protect digital evidence from magnetic fields, moisture, dust, vibration, or any other elements that may damage or destroy it.
All potential sources of digital evidence, such as removable storage media (e.g., CD, DVD, flash drives) should also be collected.

All computers, computer components or computer media that potentially contain digital evidence shall be booked into the Property Room as soon as possible to avoid damage from extreme temperatures, humidity, static electricity, strong magnetic fields or exposure to other items which could damage the evidence.
All devices or media containing digital evidence shall be booked in the manner described in Directive 304.1/8.9 – DIGITAL EVIDENCE.

Due to the volume of criminal investigations involving cellular phones, as well as the substantial amount of time it takes to process this evidence, officers shall use the following procedure when any cellular device is collected as evidence.
If the device is powered off, leave the device off to reduce the risk of the device connecting to a network.
If the device is powered on:
Place device in Airplane Mode or remove SIM card to prevent remote data wiping
Keep the device on and charged to prevent erasing of encryption keys
When possible, obtain the password from the owner or person in possession of the cell phone before it was collected.
In instances where the owner of a device has signed consent for a phone to be processed, the phone will be released to the owner upon completion.
In all instances where a device has been seized as evidence, all devices shall be either:

blocks.label: (a)
blocks.text: Booked in the Toledo Police Department Property Room

blocks.label: (b)
blocks.text: Booked in a temporary storage locker located in one of the Investigative Service Division offices, or

blocks.label: (c)
blocks.text: Given directly to a detective in the Digital Forensics Office.
All devices seized as evidence shall be placed in either a paper or clear plastic bag with a completed evidence tag.
All submitted requests require a completed Digital Forensics Request for Analysis form (61.8), The following is also required unless the owner of the device is deceased:
Legal Process to extract the contents of the device or
A Consent Form signed by the owner of the device
DIGITAL PHOTOGRAPHS BY DEPARTMENT EMPLOYEES

The department has digital cameras to assist officers in documenting crime scenes, accident scenes, evidence, injuries, RRE incidents and other items or events. Photographs from these incidents are evidence and shall be handled as such. Officers using digital cameras shall use the following procedure:
Officers taking the photographs shall complete the front of the PHOTO PLACARD.
Officers shall photograph the front of the PHOTO PLACARD, making it the first picture in the series of photographs.

Upon completion of photographing the incident, officers shall complete the back of the PHOTO PLACARD, and then photograph the back of the PHOTO PLACARD, making it the final photograph in the series of photographs.
The memory card containing the images and the completed PHOTO PLACARD shall be placed in a MEMORY CARD ENVELOPE (TPD FORM 25.5).
Memory cards shall only contain images from a single incident. Officers shall use separate memory cards and PHOTO PLACARDS for each incident where photographs are required.
Only one (1) memory card and PHOTO PLACARD shall be placed in each MEMORY CARD ENVELOPE, unless multiple memory cards are used to photograph a single incident.
The memory card and the completed PHOTO PLACARD shall be booked, prior to the end of the officer’s shift, in the manner described in Directive 304.1/8.9 – DIGITAL EVIDENCE.
Digital photograph images will be handled as evidence and processed in an expedient manner.
Only officers assigned to the Video Office, and authorized by the commander of the Property Investigations Section, shall download images stored on memory cards.
The images shall only be downloaded to the secure computer designated for photographic evidence.
After the digital photographic images have been transferred to the secure computer, the memory cards will be formatted and returned to the appropriate bureau, section or unit.

Officers requesting photographic prints shall complete a VIDEO OFFICE WORK ORDER (TPD FORM 31.13). The VIDEO OFFICE WORK ORDER shall be submitted to the Video Office no later than four (4) workdays prior to the date the photographic prints are needed.
Video Office personnel will process the VIDEO OFFICE WORK ORDER, make the necessary prints, and forward them to the requesting officer.
AUDIO AND VIDEO RECORDINGS MADE BY DEPARTMENT PERSONNEL

The department utilizes audio or video equipment to assist officers in documenting crime scenes, accident scenes, evidence, injuries, RRE incidents and other items or events. Any such recordings from these incidents are evidence and shall be handled as such. Officers shall document in the CRIME REPORT or SUPPLEMENTAL CRIME REPORT (TPD FORM 38.2) the date, time and location the recording was made, and the name of the officer making the recording. Officers making such recordings shall use the following procedure:
Officers making such recordings shall clearly label the recording media as evidence.
The recording media shall be properly packaged and booked in the manner described in Directive 304.1/8.9 – DIGITAL EVIDENCE.
Officers shall book all audio and video recordings prior to the end of the officer’s shift.
AUDIO AND VIDEO EVIDENCE FROM OTHER SOURCES

Any audio or video recording of an evidentiary nature not made by department personnel shall be appropriately tagged, marked, or labeled and booked in the manner described in Directive 304.1/8.9 – DIGITAL EVIDENCE. Analysis and/or duplication services of audio or video recordings shall be performed by the Video Office. Requests for analysis and/or duplication services shall be made utilizing the TOLEDO POLICE VIDEO OFFICE WORK ORDER (TPD FORM 31.13).
SUBMITTING EVIDENCE FOR FORENSIC ANALYSIS

The officer in charge of an investigation is responsible for requesting lab examinations for any evidence concerning his case. When available, officers shall submit materials or substances (e.g., hairs, fibers, paint, glass, flammables, shoe prints) from a known source for comparison with physical evidence collected. Requests for examination shall be made by completing a REQUEST FOR ANALYSIS (TPD FORM 61.5). A REQUEST FOR ANALYSIS form shall be completed for each lab or office performing any analysis.

If the forensic analysis will be conducted by a lab other than the Toledo Police Department Forensic Lab or Computer Crimes Office, the officer requesting the analysis shall also complete a CRIME SCENE INVESTIGATION UNIT – REQUEST FOR SERVICES form to request the transfer of the evidence to the appropriate lab. The CRIME SCENE INVESTIGATION UNIT – REQUEST FOR SERVICES form shall specify which lab the officer is requesting to perform the analysis. Officers may also be required to complete additional forms per the policy of the other lab. The original of each form shall be forwarded to the Records Section and copies sent to the appropriate lab and the Crime Scene Investigation Unit.

To promote the safe handling of evidence by lab/office personnel, the location where the evidence was found shall be noted on the REQUEST FOR ANALYSIS form. If the origin of the evidence is unknown, this fact shall also be noted on the form. REQUESTS FOR ANALYSIS that do not state the source of the evidence shall be returned to the requesting officer, through his section commander.
Lab/office personnel shall provide written reports detailing the findings of all analyses conducted.

When a suspect is in custody and a forensic sample is needed for forensic laboratory analysis (buccal [oral] swabs, blood, head and/or pubic hairs), one (1) of the following needs to be obtained and presented to the on-duty nurse at the Lucas County Corrections Center (LCCC) by an investigator:
A court order.
A search warrant.
An appropriately completed and signed waiver of search obtained by the investigator.
An officer of the same sex as the prisoner shall be present at the time the samples are obtained.

blocks.label: (a)
blocks.text: The officer present during the collection shall ensure that all evidence is properly packaged, sealed, and labeled with all the reference and identification information needed for chain-of custody purposes. The Forensic Lab will supply special envelopes to the LCCC for this purpose.

blocks.label: (b)
blocks.text: The officer shall also document in a SUPPLEMENTAL CRIME REPORT what was observed in the collection process and the steps that were taken to preserve the chain of custody.

blocks.label: (c)
blocks.text: The officer is responsible for the chain of custody and submission of the evidence to the Property Management Unit.
The following information should be conveyed to the LCCC nurse when requesting forensic samples:

Hair samples: If hair samples are required (whether from the head or pubic area) it is imperative that at least 50 hair samples be obtained by plucking and not cutting the hair, and should be obtained from various areas in the affected region.
Buccal swabs: If buccal swabs are required, at least two (2) swabs should be obtained by rolling the swab on the inside of the cheek, one for the right cheek and one for the left cheek.
DRYING ROOM

The Drying Room may be utilized for drying evidentiary items that contain blood or other body fluid to prepare these items for laboratory examination. The administrative responsibility for this area shall rest with the Crime Scene Investigation Unit commander.

The Drying Room shall be locked at all times, except when in use by authorized personnel. Access to this area shall be limited to officers booking property, forensic lab personnel, evidence technicians and/or investigators. A key for the Drying Room is located at the Investigations Bureau desk. Officers utilizing the key shall complete the entry on the DRYING ROOM KEY LOG (TPD FORM 28.1).
All personnel entering the Drying Room shall record the required information on the DRYING ROOM LOG (TPD FORM 28.2).

Property placed in the Drying Room shall be handled in a manner to preserve its evidentiary value and prevent cross contamination. Property shall be properly tagged and laid out on clean brown craft paper, which is available in the room.
The Crime Scene Investigation Unit commander shall determine when property placed in the Drying Room is to be moved to the Property Room.
It shall be the responsibility of the Crime Scene Investigation Unit commander to maintain the completed copies of the DRYING ROOM KEY LOG and DRYING ROOM LOG.
FIREARMS
See Directive 304.1/8.4 – FIREARMS IN CUSTODY
HANDLING OF DNA EVIDENCE

Officers responding to a crime scene which is found to contain body fluids (e.g., blood, semen, saliva, urine, feces, vomit), shall attempt to locate and protect physical evidence and determine the need for an evidence technician. Officers should practice the following universal safety precautions:
Assume all biological materials are contaminated.
Assume all individuals are infectious or contagious.
Officers shall use the appropriate personal protection equipment (PPE) (e.g., gloves, masks, protective outerwear, shoe covers, surgical caps).

Officers shall contact the on-duty Investigations Bureau supervisor when potential DNA evidence has been discovered. If officers are directed to collect the evidence, they shall adhere to the guidelines established by the basic training curriculum of the Ohio Peace Officer Training Commission.
The following evidence handling protocols shall be observed:
Never seal moist articles in plastic.
Items shall be placed in clean paper bags or boxes.
Package each item separately and do not use staples.
Attach the proper tag to each container.
If necessary, mark containers “Biohazard” and identify the hazard.
Place dry items in the Property Room or one of the Night Property Rooms.
Wet items shall be placed in the Drying Room.
Wet items shall be completely air-dried before being packaged and booked in the Property Room or Night Property Rooms.

Potential DNA evidence collected at crime scenes shall be completely documented in the CRIME REPORT or SUPPLEMENTAL CRIME REPORT. The assigned investigator shall determine what specific forensic examinations will be requested.

Evidence that needs forensic testing shall be submitted to the nearest Bureau of Criminal Investigation and Identification (BCI&I) accredited laboratory. If the necessary testing is of a specialized nature not provided by BCI&I, prior permission from the Lucas County Prosecutor’s office and the Investigative Services Bureau commander is required.

Evidence that is to be processed by BCI&I personnel shall be submitted through the Crime Scene Investigative Unit. A CRIME SCENE INVESTIGATION UNIT – REQUEST FOR SERVICES (TPD FORM 28.8) AND A REQUEST FOR ANALYSIS (TPD FORM 61.5) shall be completed. The original of each form shall be forwarded to the Records Section and copies sent to the appropriate lab and the Crime Scene Investigation Unit.

The commander of the Crime Scene Investigation Unit, or his designee, shall transport all necessary evidence to BCI&I on a timely basis. The evidence shall be receipted from the Property Room to Evidence Receiving at BCI&I. The evidence submission sheet shall be maintained in the Crime Scene Investigation Unit file to document the chain of custody. All evidence shall be logged at the Crime Scene Investigation Unit to document its departure to and arrival from BCI&I. Crime Scene Investigation Unit personnel shall maintain this log to verify the chain of custody for each case and to record yearly submissions to BCI&I.

summary: Revised March 2026. At a major scene with Investigations and CSIU responding, your job is to **protect the scene**. At every other scene, you are the evidence technician: dust for prints with your issued kit, collect what you can, and request CSIU services on TPD 28.8 for anything beyond you.

The directive's most practical content is the handling rules that keep evidence from being destroyed: biological evidence goes in paper and never sealed wet in plastic; computers are not touched, searched or powered on, and the plug gets pulled from the CPU case; cell phones stay off if off, and go in airplane mode and stay charged if on.
Everything digital (photos, recordings, devices) is evidence and gets booked before end of shift under 304.1/8.9.
must: Protect the scene and any potential physical evidence when Investigations and CSIU are responding to a major crime (3.1)

Process other scenes for fingerprints yourself with your issued kit; label the back of each lift card with the Records number, date and time, exact location of the lift, your initials and ID, and handle it as evidence (3.2.1a)
Collect items that cannot be processed at the scene, protect them for prints, package in paper when possible, and book them; protect items too large to move at the scene (3.2.1b, c)
Complete a CSIU Request for Services (TPD 28.8) in every instance you need CSIU work (AFIS search, latent processing), original to Records and a copy to CSIU (2, 3.2.2)
Contact the Computer Crimes Office before seizing anything on a network or business mainframe, or before executing a search warrant on one (4.1)

On a computer seizure: clear everyone, including officers, away from the keyboard, mouse and case; disconnect network and phone lines; record and photograph what is on the screen; pull the power cord from the CPU case (not the wall); photograph and sketch the setup; seize manuals, notes and post-its; label connectors; transport in the back seat away from the trunk radio; book promptly (4.2)
Pull the plug immediately if the screen shows data being deleted or overwritten (4.2.6 note)

Cell phones: if off, leave it off. If on, put it in airplane mode or pull the SIM and keep it on and charged. Try to get the passcode from the owner before collecting. Bag it in paper or clear plastic with an evidence tag, and book it in the Property Room, an ISD temporary locker, or hand it directly to a Digital Forensics detective (4.3)
Submit a Digital Forensics Request for Analysis (61.8) plus legal process or a signed owner consent form for any phone extraction, unless the owner is deceased (4.3.7)

Department photos: fill out the front of the Photo Placard and shoot it first, complete the back and shoot it last, one memory card and placard per incident, into a Memory Card Envelope (TPD 25.5), booked before end of shift (5.1)
Document the date, time, location and recording officer of any department audio or video in the Crime or Supplemental Report, label it as evidence, and book it before end of shift (6.1)
Contact the on-duty Investigations Bureau supervisor when potential DNA evidence is found, and treat all biological material as contaminated and all people as infectious; use PPE (11, 11.1)

Package biological evidence in clean paper bags or boxes, each item separately, no staples, tagged, marked Biohazard if needed; dry items to the Property Room, wet items to the Drying Room and completely air-dried before booking (11.2)
Document potential DNA evidence fully in the Crime or Supplemental Report (11.3)

Complete a Request for Analysis (TPD 61.5) for each lab doing work, state where the evidence was found (or that the origin is unknown), and submit known-source comparison samples when available (8.1, 8.2)
Log in on the Drying Room Key Log (TPD 28.1) and Drying Room Log (TPD 28.2), and lay items on clean brown craft paper (9.2 to 9.4)
never: Seal moist articles in plastic (11.2)
Open a CPU case without Computer Crimes Office personnel present (4.2.1)
Search a computer for evidence, turn it on or off, or accept the suspect's help shutting it down or saving files (4.2.2, 4.2.3)
Store seized computer components in the trunk near the radio transmitter if the back seat is at all possible (4.2.10)
Download memory card images yourself; only authorized Video Office officers do that, onto the secure photo evidence computer (5.2.1, 5.2.2)
Submit a Request for Analysis without the evidence source; it comes back through your section commander (8.2)
notes: A computer that looks tampered with could be booby trapped; notify the Technical Services Section commander (4)
Vehicles in major crimes needing CSIU processing get towed to the Impound Lot and protected inside if needed (3.2.1b exception)
AFIS entry and all fingerprint identifications are done by CSIU (3.3)

In-custody forensic samples (buccal swabs, blood, hair) require a court order, search warrant or signed waiver presented to the LCCC nurse by an investigator, with a same-sex officer present who documents the collection in a Supplemental and owns the chain of custody. Hair: at least 50 plucked, not cut. Buccal: at least two swabs, one per cheek (8.4)
Analysis by a lab other than TPD Forensic Lab or Computer Crimes also needs a CSIU Request for Services specifying the lab; BCI submissions go through CSIU with both forms (8.1, 11.5)
Specialized testing BCI does not offer requires prior permission from the Lucas County Prosecutor and the ISB commander (11.4)
Photo prints: Video Office Work Order (TPD 31.13) at least four workdays ahead. Outside audio and video is also booked under 304.1/8.9 and duplicated only by the Video Office (5.3, 7)
Firearms in custody: see 304.1/8.4 (10)

blocks.text: Policy

It is the policy of the Toledo Police Department to respond to unusual circumstances such as natural and man-made disasters in an effective manner. In these situations, the department's goal is to protect life and property and to restore order. Coordination and deployment of resources shall be in compliance with the provisions of the Toledo-Lucas County Emergency Operations Plan.
Procedures
PLANNING RESPONSIBILITY

Since the majority of the department's response during an unusual occurrence originates within the Operations Division, the Operations Division commander shall be responsible for the department's operational response. The communications/all-hazards liaison shall be responsible for developing the department’s emergency operation plans.
COMMUNICATIONS

One of the most vital needs during a disaster is effective communications. This includes the notification and mobilization process as well as coordinated communications among Operations Division personnel.
During any emergency, Communications serves as the intermediate coordinator of activity and information. Communications’ primary responsibilities include:
Establishment of an emergency operations talkgroup, if needed.
Continued management of calls for service from the public.
Prompt notifications to concerned agencies throughout the period of the emergency.
Maintenance of a communications log during the incident.
EMERGENCY ALERT SYSTEM

In the event of an emergency or serious incident that requires immediate dissemination of information to the public at large; the department may utilize the Emergency Alert System (EAS). The EAS is comprised of regional radio and television stations that have agreed to interrupt their commercial broadcasts to alert the public.

Only the chief of police or his designee may authorize access to the EAS. In the absence of the chief of police, or his designee, the on-duty shift commander from the appropriate geographical area, after exhausting all efforts to contact the chief or his designee, may authorize activation of the system.
Officers on the scene of an incident in which the EAS is being considered shall provide communications personnel sufficient facts to accurately describe the nature of the emergency.
In order to activate the EAS, contact the Lucas County Sheriff’s Office dispatch center - (419) 213-4977.
The mayor and the safety director of the City of Toledo and the Lucas County Sheriff shall all be notified of the activation of the EAS.
REMOVED
EMERGENCY OPERATIONS CENTER

The Emergency Operations Center (EOC) may be activated at the direction of the chief of police, or his designee. The EOC shall coordinate emergency services throughout the duration of the emergency. The chief of police may also assign the public information officer (PIO) to assist during the emergency. The PIO shall be responsible for all news releases.
ALERT STAGES

Different occurrences require different levels of response to protect lives and property and to restore order. When unusual circumstances rise to the level that require the mobilization of additional or off-duty personnel, after evaluating the need for additional personnel, supervisors should consider utilizing one or more of the following alert stages.
Stage One – Hold on-duty personnel past their normal quitting time.
Stage Two – Bring personnel from the next shift in before their normal starting time.
Stage Three – Activate Call-Back “Plan A”. See Directive 408.1/3.4 – CALL-BACK PLANS.
Stage Four – Activate Call-Back “Plan B”. See Directive 408.1/3.4 – CALL-BACK PLANS.
The emergency call-back plan is a general guideline to meet the needs of the department, depending upon the nature and magnitude of the emergency.
The chief of police, or his designee, shall make the final determination for the implementation or cessation of the emergency call-back plan.

The on-duty Operations Division shift commander shall be responsible for notifying the chief of police, through the chain of command, whenever an emergency of sufficient magnitude arises that may require additional personnel.
At the direction of the chief of police, notification shall be made to the safety director and the mayor.
FLEXIBILITY DURING AN EMERGENCY

The initial response to an emergency and implementation of a call-back plan must take into consideration the nature of the emergency, manpower requirements, time of day, and expected duration of the crisis.

It may be determined that it would be more expedient to hold over the onduty shift in order to handle immediate manpower needs or to order the following shift’s regularly scheduled personnel in early.
The emergency call-back plan does not preclude other administrative options of staffing for an emergency or the temporary reassignment of department personnel.
EMERGENCY CALL-BACK LOG
Each division commander or their designee shall be responsible for maintaining a printed version of their respective EMERGENCY CALL-BACK LOG.
The hard copies of the EMERGENCY CALL-BACK LOG shall be maintained in a book that is readily accessible and identifiable to others in an emergency situation.

The printed version shall be updated twice a year or as personnel changes necessitate. It shall contain the names of every person assigned to each section by rank, in seniority order, and shall include addresses and telephone numbers.

blocks.label: (a)
blocks.text: REMOVED

blocks.label: (b)
blocks.text: REMOVED

blocks.label: (c)
blocks.text: Accurate information is vital during an emergency. Officers are reminded that Directive 201.4/8 – CHANGES OF PERSONAL INFORMATION, requires that a City of Toledo Personnel Action Form (PAF-1) be completed whenever there is a change of name, address, phone number and/or marital status.
CALL-BACK PLANS
There are two emergency mobilization call-back plans, "Plan A" and "Plan B."
“Plan A” is based on the regularly scheduled shifts at the respective district stations. However, all regularly scheduled days off and training days will be cancelled.
“Plan B” is formulated around two, twelve hour shifts.

blocks.label: (a)
blocks.text: Sworn supervisor roll-call times are 0600 hours for days, and 1800 hours for nights.

blocks.label: (b)
blocks.text: Patrolman roll-call times are 0630 and 0730 hours for days and 1830 and 1930 hours for nights.
IMPLEMENTATION OF CALL-BACK PLAN

Once an emergency call-back plan has been authorized by the chief of police, the onduty Operations shift commanders, or their designees, shall immediately assign a detail of supervisors to recall the first affected shift.
Recall shall begin with the shift commanders and work through the other sworn supervisors and patrol officers assigned to that shift.
Officers shall be told where and when to report. If possible, roll-call times will remain unchanged for each shift if “Plan A” is implemented. Once completed, the next affected shift shall be called.
If the decision to utilize “Plan B” is made, the shift presently on duty will remain on duty as long as necessary to effect a smooth transition to 12 hour shifts.
The ultimate goal of this plan is to keep the day shift on days, the night shift on nights and the remaining shifts divided between days or nights as necessary.

If at all possible, assignments should be given at roll calls. However, in the absence of other instructions, all emergency personnel, equipment and supplies shall be directed to the operations staging area.
CANCELING VACATIONS, LEAVES
Generally, vacation, OT, and other special days off (e.g., funeral leave, jury duty) will not be cancelled without specific instruction from the chief of police.
METHODS OF CONTACTING OFFICERS
The method of contacting officers will depend on the nature of the emergency.
The telephone, cell phone, email, ISE generated text message or department radio will be the initial methods used to contact officers.
Radio and television stations may be utilized to air the recall order as directed by the chief of police or his designee.
Supervisors may utilize additional methods to contact unreachable officers.
TESTING OF CALL-BACK PLAN
Only the chief of police or his designee shall initiate a test of the emergency call-back plan.
Upon determining the scope of the test, the chief of police, or his designee, shall notify the affected commanders and advise them to conduct a test recall of their personnel.

blocks.label: (a)
blocks.text: Supervisors shall utilize their EMERGENCY CALL-BACK LOG to contact their personnel.

blocks.label: (b)
blocks.text: Supervisors shall utilize all available resources so that all off-duty personnel are contacted.

blocks.label: (c)
blocks.text: When contacting off-duty personnel, a supervisor shall:
Contact all off-duty personnel except those off sick or injured.
Advise that a test is being conducted.

Ask the officer, if this were a real emergency situation, how long it would take him to report for duty. If an employee states that he would be unable to report for duty, the reason given shall be documented.
Record the time contact is made.
If an answering machine is reached, the supervisor shall leave a message notifying the employee of the test and advise him to call back within the time limit of the test.
A separate phone number should be designated and staffed for officers to respond back to the department.
If the employee responds before the end of the test, he shall be marked as contacted.
If there is no response, or if the officer responds after the time limit, he shall be listed as not contacted.
Incorrect or disconnected telephone numbers shall be recorded.

blocks.label: (d)
blocks.text: Supervisors can make a second phone call attempt during the test recall. No calls shall be made after the test has concluded.

blocks.label: (e)
blocks.text: Upon completion of the test, the section commander conducting the test shall complete the EMERGENCY CALL-BACK TEST SUMMARY (TPD FORM 20.13) and forward the original and copies as directed on the form.
The Planning, Research and Inspections Section shall coordinate the testing of the call-back plan, compile the data and complete an analysis of the test recall.
The testing of the call-back plan shall be completed twice a year.
EQUIPMENT DISTRIBUTION
During an emergency mobilization for a disaster or other situation, departmental equipment must be distributed in an efficient manner.

All Operations Division personnel who respond to an emergency mobilization shall ensure they have all of their issued equipment. If necessary, the property management unit shall be contacted by the incident commander (IC) to obtain additional equipment.
All officers recalled during an emergency shall report for duty in the prescribed uniform.
TRANSPORTATION REQUIREMENTS

The nature of a disaster will determine the methods needed to provide for transportation of personnel to their assigned areas. In addition to police department vehicles, other methods to be used may include, but are not limited to, the following:
Other city department vehicles
TARTA
Military vehicles
Private carriers
SPECIAL TASK FORCES

The chief of police or his designated commander may request that a special task force be formed to address a specific emergency mobilization need. A department supervisor shall take command of any special task force.
The special task force shall be given a specific mission to accomplish.
The task force supervisor shall report progress through the chain of command.
ROLE OF OTHER BUREAUS

Depending on the nature of the emergency, additional manpower needs may arise in other bureaus within the department. Each respective division commander shall review manpower needs within his areas of concern during the course of the emergency incident.
Utilization of established recall procedures should be considered initially.

If the use of non-uniformed personnel is necessary, an effort should be made to readily identify plain-clothes officers to the public. This may be accomplished by use of reflective police vests, nametags or other means of identification.
EMERGENCY OPERATIONS PLAN
The department’s emergency operations plan consists of a separate manual containing specific procedures for the following:
All Hazards Response
Aircraft Disaster
Bomb Threats
Bomb Scene Management
Terrorism
Hazardous Materials
Civil Disturbance
Mass Arrests
Tornados
Urban Flooding
Winter Storms
Main Post Office Bio-Detection Alarm Response
Tactical Interoperable Communications
Emerging Infectious Diseases
Emergency Evacuations
Dangerous Wild Animals
Active Shooter Response
Mutual Aid Response
Toledo Police Facilities Emergency Response
All sworn personnel shall be familiar with the emergency operations plan.
INCIDENT COMMAND SYSTEM

The Toledo Police Department utilizes the incident command system (ICS) as a method of managing personnel and resources engaged in incidents, emergencies, and disasters. Given the magnitude of events, it's not always possible for any one agency to handle the management and resource needs (e.g., personnel, equipment). Other agencies and disciplines might be required to bring the incident to a successful resolution. These agencies must work together in a coordinated effort under the same management system. ICS is a management tool designed to control emergency operations by establishing functional areas under the direction of an incident commander.

Supervisors responding to an incident shall determine when formal activation of the ICS is appropriate. Supervisors should consider formal activation of ICS for all critical incidents. Some examples of critical incidents are:
Barricaded suspect or hostage incidents
Fires
Natural disasters, such as tornadoes, floods, ice storms or earthquakes
Human and animal disease outbreaks
Search and rescue missions
Hazardous materials incidents
Criminal acts and crime scene investigations
Terrorist incidents, including the use of weapons of mass destruction
Events of national interest (e.g., presidential visits)
Other planned events (e.g., parades, sporting events, concerts, demonstrations)
Command protocol and procedures of the ICS shall be followed in accordance with training guidelines.
The department shall provide training of agency personnel in the use of ICS.
The department shall conduct annual training for department personnel on the emergency operation plans to include ICS.
The department shall conduct a biennial exercise to test the department’s response capabilities as it pertains to the emergency response plans and ICS.
AFTER-ACTION REPORT

Following the department's involvement in a disaster situation or other emergency operation, the IC shall submit an after-action report through the chain of command to the Operations Division commander within ten workdays after the conclusion of the incident, or as directed. See Directive 104.1/6 – AFTER-ACTION REPORT.
Policy

The Toledo Police Department considers the preservation of life to be the primary consideration when dealing with hostage/barricaded subject situations. All reasonable efforts should be made to achieve a peaceful end to these situations, including negotiation with the subject as well as the use of alternative approaches and tactics. All personnel involved in these incidents shall work in a cooperative effort to resolve the incident in a safe and efficient manner. Reasonable efforts will be used to avoid confrontation in favor of controlling and containing the situation until the arrival of trained tactical and/or critical incident negotiation personnel.
Definitions

A barricaded subject is an individual who denies access to police or other emergency response personnel through the use, or threatened use, of force, weapons, or physical impediments preventing entry into a location where the services provided by such agencies have been requested, or are required by law.
Any person held by another against his will by force or threat of force, expressed or implied.
Procedures
GENERAL GUIDELINES
Physical Control Techniques shall be governed by Directive 103.2 – RESPONSE TO RESISTANCE.
Firearms discipline: officers shall not discharge weapons at the scene unless lawfully ordered to do so or when defending themselves or others.
If the incident involves a pursuit, Directive 401.1 – PURSUIT OPERATIONS is applicable to that portion of the incident.
Communications, orders, and actions during a barricaded subject or hostage incident must be clear, coordinated, and conveyed to all personnel involved.

Each hostage incident will present its own unique set of circumstances. Although certain operational guidelines will be applicable to most situations, officers may be required to use ingenuity and resourcefulness when utilizing those guidelines to arrive at a successful outcome.

If an officer is taken hostage, the officer may be at the mercy of an armed suspect who has the advantage, but experience has shown that giving up the officer’s firearm upon demand does not reduce the danger. Surrendering the firearm might mean giving away the officer’s only chance for survival; therefore, an officer should use every tactical tool at their disposal to avoid surrendering the firearm.

When a law enforcement officer has been taken hostage, the officer’s efforts at independent action must be anticipated. The Incident Commander (IC) and critical incident negotiator must, as soon as possible, attempt to determine if any officer is held hostage and evaluate the officer’s ability to take action.

When hostages have been held for a substantial period, experience has shown that they may develop sympathies for their captors (Stockholm Syndrome). Officers should not fail to consider the effects of psychological pressures on the hostages, and assess the likelihood that they will shield their captors. The hostages may, in fact, willingly conceal suspects among themselves upon release. As the period of time grows longer, the chance of such behavior occurring increases.
The safety of hostages can best be assured by preventing their removal from the scene by the suspect.
INCIDENT PRIORITIES
Incident priorities are the preservation of life, incident stabilization, and the preservation of property.

Although the preservation of life is the highest priority, officers must balance the Department’s incident priorities with a person’s rights when considering police action. Absent a hostage or other endangered individuals, and if no crime has been committed that necessitates the custody of the subject, the Incident Commander may decline to enter a structure or effect an arrest. An example of an incident where this option may be employed is a noncompliant, suicidal, barricaded subject when only the subject may be endangered.
It is the determination of the Incident Commander whether exigent circumstances exist to enter a structure or take action to effect an arrest in a barricaded subject or hostage situation.

The Incident Commander shall confer with the on-scene SWAT Commander before entry or arrest to determine whether the action taken would create greater danger to all persons present than taking no action.
The totality of the circumstances shall be considered when determining exigency, and when deciding to take action or decline action in a barricaded subject or hostage situation.
The juvenile status of a subject shall be considered when determining whether a crime has been committed or if the subject is the only person with standing to consent to entry into the structure.
RESPONSIBILITIES
RESPONSIBILITIES OF THE OFFICERS ON THE SCENE
Officers arriving first on the scene should carefully analyze the tactical situation and determine if immediate intervention is appropriate.
If the hostage taker has not gained physical control of the scene, immediate intervention may be appropriate.

If the suspect has gained control of the crime scene, immediate intervention may increase the danger to the hostage. Therefore, officers are advised to contain and control the scene pending the arrival of trained Tactical Operations Team and Critical Incident Negotiation Team personnel.
